MY PROFESSOR. He gave me a rose, And he said, "Can you read The alphabet dewy-eyed Flora invented (So daintily tinted and charmingly scented) To write over valley and mead?" Do you think—m.l,k be—that he means to propose? Ctr why should he give me the eloquent rose? For it is, you know, Love's sweet intercessor. And soft were his eves, and so tenderly beaming, 'lhey thrilled me and stirred all my heart into dreaming Of him—the august professor. And I dreamed (was it bold?) that he meant to propose, So tender his words when he gave me the rose. I shall not be coy And coquettish, or shy, When he seeks me again. Only trifling," you say? But I know he is earnest and true as the day; And his prayers how can I deny? For I feel—l am sure—that he means to propose, Such presage of bliss is the gift of a rose. C. W. THAYER.

..... The man, says one of the early Greek philosophers, who is not content with little is content with nothing. General Washington stopped at an hotel with a squad of subordinate officers, and attracted the attention of an Irish servant. Pat was very attentive to the General, and prompty attended to his every wish. The General observed the Irishman gazing at him and his officers as they were about departing, and asked Pat "How he liked the look of his boys?" "Well, yer honour," replied Pat, "I'm not competent to judge of the stars in the resence of the sun." Constance is very young, but she is also better worth quoting than most grown people. Her envy was some- what aroused by the fact that a wedding was about to take place in the family of her little playmate, and that the playmate thereby had the advantage of her; so she remarked, very complacently, to her little friend's mamma; "Mrs. —, did you know that I was engaged to be married?" "Why, no, Conny. Is that, so?' "Yes, ma'am; I'm engaged to Fritz Ward" (small boy of her acquaintance). "He doesn't know it, but I've got to explain it to him." "Well, Conny, do you exp ct to be married soon?" "Well, I hope so. The fact is, I'm tired of being spanked, and I think we'll be married very soon." THE Hrur-ToxED OFFICE Boy.—A Roston lawyer has had under his eye of late, in the case of his office boy, an interesting instance of the influence upon the rising generation of the reading of romantic literature. Not long ago the lawyer advertised for an office boy, and employed a bright-looking youth of fourteen, solely on his own recommendation, partly because he liked the boy's looks and partly because he was impressed by his name, which was Arthur Hamilton Montague. The boy turned out well, in spite of a propensity for reading rain- bow-covered literature in his spare moments, and the- lawyer found it an unalloyed pleasure to be able to sum- mon an Arthur Hamilton Montague and send him trot- ting off on an errand. One day, after the boy had beenin the office about a month, the outer door opened one afternoon when Arthur Hamilton Montague happened to be out, and a sturdy and elderly Irish woman, in a faded shawl and straw bonnet, came peeping furtively through the door of the inner office. "I ax yer pardon, sorr," she said, when she saw the lawyer; "but is this L'y'ar Faywarthy's office ?" "It is." "Sure, an' I thought so. And can ye tell me sorr" (glancing under the table and then up toward the top of the bookcase), "if me boy' Mickey is annvwhere about, sorr ?" " Your boy Mickey ! I There's no boy Mickey here. Madam." "Sure, an' he's the office boy of L'y'ar Faywarthy, son." "You've made a mistake, madam. Our office boy is named Arthur 1 Hamilton Montague." The woman looked aghast for an I instant, and then burst into a convulsive laughter. "Arthur Hamilton Mcntague I is it, indade !" she ex- claimed between her spasms oilaughter. "Sure then the b'y's me own choild, 'an' his name is Mickey Halligan, none the less, sorr." Confronted on his return with the visit of the inquiring woman. Arthur Hamilton Mon- tague was compelled to admit the relationship. He said he had got his official name, so to speak, out of no less than three novels, and felt that he was fairly entitled to it. —Boston Transcript. "THE TOWN OF THE EMPIRE."—A correspondent of rEvenernent, writing from the Rhenish Prussian town of Essen (or Essen-Krupp, as it is more commonly called by its inhabitants), gives some interesting details as to tee growth and develapment of the celebrated Krupp cast- steel manufactory, so renowned for its war materiel dur- ing the last 30 years. In 1855 it gave employment to about 800 workmen, but from statistics prepared by the I director of the works at the close of the last commercial I year of the company, it is ascertained that very few short I of 20,000 are now employed, which includes several thousand miners. Of the many furnaces which this immensefaurindire contains, 11 are incessantly alight, devouring each day 3,100 tons of coal, and producing 1,500 tons of steel. The network of rails which is laid extends over 50 kilometres, and the rolling stock consists of 38 locomotives and 883 waggons. The town of Essen is populated by 65,381 inhabitants, 13,220 of whom are children attending school, so that it may be assumed the Krupp factory provides the means of subsistence for the. majority of the population. So impressed was the Emperor by the industry when he visited Essen in 1877 that he designated it as "the town of the Empire." Of course, the Krupp factory has its memorable anecdote, already a legend in the town the outline of which is familiar to almost every schoolboy in this country. It is to the effect that the Emperor William, while passing through the workshops, stopped ' in front of the formidable hammer, "Notre Fritz," sixty metres high, and which falls on a block of iroi weighing 1 twenty thousand hundredweight. M. Krupp, in intro- I ducing the workman whose duty it was to guide the 1 colossal hammer, added. "Be is so adroit, and the course , of the stamper is so skilfully regulated that he can bring it to bay within a hair's breadth of the object placed in the centre of the iron block." The Emperor manifesting a certain incredulity, deposited his watch immediately under the hammer, and when the mechanician hesitated M. Krupp said, quoting the inscription which crosses the brow of the immense piece of machinery," Va, Fritz, frappe toujaurs." The effort was successful, and the watch, which the Emperor presented to the workman, marks to this day the hour, while the hammer falls and re-falls heavily on the steel, an impressive picture of the uniform brutality of military power. UNEXPECTED ANSWERS.—The girls are not a whit behind, or before, the boys in malapropos answers. For example, when a little girl was asked the reason why the Israelites made a golden calf, she replied: "'Cause they hadna? as muckle siller as would mak' a coo." ' Another Scotch girl, at an examination, gave a , pretty definition when asked," What does patience mean? " "Wait a wee an' dinna weary." During a School Board examination in the west of Scotland, the examiner asked a little girl, "What is meant by He was amply ' rewarded?"—" Paid for't." —" No, no. You are quite wrong. Suppose you were to go into a baker's shop and buy a half-quarter loaf, and lay down fourpence, would you say you had amply rewarded the baker ?" Unhesi- tatingly the girl replied in the affirmative. " Why ?"—: "Because the loaf's only twopence three-farthings," was the unlooked-for answer. The inspector let that girl off easily during the remainder of the lesson. A little fellow was sent a message by his mother to a lady. When he had delivered it, he did not seem in a hurry to go; and] the lady, noticing this, asked him if there was anything' else his mother had bidden him say. She was not I prepared for his reply: "She said I wasna to seek onything for coming, but if ye gave me onything, I was to tak' it." Sunday School stories are sometimes equal to others in their irresistible fun. Sacred things have an influence over the mind of youth; but occa- sionally, as in the following anecdote, the influence or temptation is too strong for the mischief-loving boys, and eventually overcomes their religious feelings for the time. A Sunday school teacher asked her scholars to learn an appropriate text to say as they gave in their pennies to the next collection. The first was, "He that giveth to the poor lendeth to the Lord ;" and all were right until it came to the last boy, who, reluctantly dropping his penny into the box, said, to the great amazement of teachers and scholars, "The fool and his money are soon parted r A father said, Bill, if you had your due, you'd get a good whipping." " I know,' daddy; but bills are not always paid when due." Equally clever was a boy hearing of the wonders of astronomy. "Men have learned the distances of the stars," his father said; "and, with their spectroscopes, found out what they are made of." "Yes," was the reply; "and isn't it strange, pa, how they found out ,Their names also ?" A legal luminary was severely dealt' with at the hands of a young lady noted fcr her sharp wit. The judge, whose personal appearance was as un- prepossessing as his intellect was keen and his judgment air, asked this female what she meant by the term humbugged." " Well, my lord," replied the lady, angry at the interruption, "I hardly know how to explain it; but if a yourur lady called your lordship a handsome man, she would be humbugging you." Even sharper was the epigrammatical reply of a young lady to an old admirer, who, having found her glove, returned it to her with the following distich : If from your glove you take the letter G Your glove is love, which I devote to thee. UM old gentleman's name was Page; and he received the following unexpected answer, which chagrined him so much that he left the place:— If from your Page you take the letter P Your Page is age, and that won't do for me.

WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CM. ANNUAL MEETING.

On Monday evening, the annual general meeting of the Warrington Football Club was held in Cairo- street Schoolroom. In the absence of the president amneillor R. W. Francornb), Councillor F. A. Roberts was elected to preside in the early part of the meeting. There were also on the platform Councillor W. Pierpoint, Mr. J. E. Warren (hon. sec.), and Mr. , T. Pemberton (hon. treasurer). There was a large attendance of members. The CHAIRMAN said it was the first time that he had taken the chair at a football meeting in Warrington, and be shoeld like to say before he sat down bow he congratulated VVarrington on putting such a team into the field as they bad often seen at Wilderspool, and how glad he was person- ally that football was making such strides in Warrington. (Applause.) He thought any of them who bad supported the Warrington Football Club would be grati- fied and satisfied with the balance sheet which had been sent to them with the notice convening the meet- ing. As in cricket and all other exercises, so it was in football, success in the balance sheet meant success in the game. If they were not succe sful in the field their balance sheet did not look nearly so well, and to make a successful balance sheet they wanted to have a successful first team at all events, and to make a successful first team they must have successful supplementary teams; and he would urge on those who were working their way into the first team to make themselves so thoroughly efficient as net only to take the place of first team men wlen they fell out, but if possible to supersede them. (Applause.)

div.head: ECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: ECRETARY'S REPORT.

The Hon. Secretary's report, which had been previously printed and circulated in pamphlet form, was taken as read. It contained among other the following items: "The season we have just brought to a close has been a very successful one from every point of view. Our first team has fully maintained the teputation acquired last season. Thirty. seven matches have been played, 21 have been won, nine lost, and seven drawn; and when it is remembered that most of the clubs played have been of the first rank, the record cannot bpt be regarded as satisfactory. The total points scored by the first team have been '26 goaln, 30 tries, and 101 minors, against 10 goals, 20 tries, and 67 minors. We have had the honour of representation on the Lancashire i county team twice this season, Fairfield Turner being ' selected on both occasiOns, and should Barnes keep up hie? form his claims cannot be ignored much longer. The 'A. ' team, notwithstanding the fact that it has been repeatedly ! weakened to fill up vacancies on the first team, has only lost four matches out of 27 played: 16 were won, and seven drawn, the total score toeing 17 goals, 32 tries, and 104 minors, to their opponents' five goals, six tries. 44 minors, Our second team has played 15 matches, nine have been won, two draws, and four lost, the total score being seven goals, 17 tries, 38 minors, to their opponents two goals, 10 tries, 32 minors. The membership of the club has increased by 110 since the last general meeting. We have now 197 ordinary members and 36 honorary. First team matches for next season have been arranged with the following clubs :—Aspull, Barrow, Free Wanderers, Moesley, Broughton, Manchester Rangers, Broughton Rangers, Rochdale Hornets, Wigan, Kendal Hornets, Kendal, Dewsbury, Oldham, Wakefield Trinity, Rugby, Halifax, Moseley (Birmingham), Heckmondwike. We have had an unusual number of accidents during the season, and on this account have been compelled on several eccaeions to meet our opponents with weak teams; but for- tunately the committee took a wise course in insuring the first and 'A.' teams against accident early in the season,and every player who has been unable to follow his employment has received 30s per week, and had his doctor's bill paid. Tee Junior Club Competition, which was inaugurated this season, although it did not unearth any 'very brilliant players, proved that there are a great many players in the town who are well worth looking after, and with a little tuition might develop into really good men. The balance derived from the competition was £3O, which was distribu- ted amongst local charitable institutions. The field, on which we have spent a large sum of money in draining, fencing, grand stand, tEc., accommodation, is considered now to be one of the beat grounas in Lancashire used for football purposes."

The How. TREASURER also submitted his statement. The abstract of general accounts for season shewed a balance of £199 5s 81- ; statement of liabilitiea and assets shewed a balance ot £299 03 81 in favour of the club. On looking through the accounts he found that the receipts for the past five seasons had been as follows:-1882-3. £34 3e lop ; 1883-4. £45 4s 2,1 ; 1884-5. £l9O 103 7d; 1885-6, £669 65 7-14 ; 1886-7, £1234 25 41. They would see from these figures what rapid strides the club bad made, and with un- animity in the future there was little doubt that the club would make still further progress, and would maintain its position as one of the leading clubs in the country. The payments, which amounted to £941 105 5d., contained items of £lO7 17a 3d, share of gate money ; £137 14s Id, dinners And refreshments to visiting teams ; 107 33., railway fares ; doctors' fees, medicine, embrocation, anklets, kneecaps, in- aurance of stand, dm, £64 10a 2d. The receipts in- cluded—£6s 155 Bd., balance in hand from last season ; gate money, Ist team, £834 14s ; "A" team and 2ad team. £165 lie 214 ; subscriptions, £59 12a. -:-On the motion of Mr..WINSTANLEY, seconded by Mr.
HARTLEY, the reports of the Secretary and Treasurer were adopted unanimously. ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.

Mr. Jogs EVANS said he had very great pleasure in pro. posing that Mr. William Pierpoint be appointed to the posi- tion of president for the ensuing year. lie was sorry Mr. Frascomb was not present to propose verbally what he had done in writing, but he was sure that in the person of Mr. Pierpoint they would have one highly efficient for the posi. tion. (Applause.)—Mr. WARREN seconded the proposition. They could not possibly, he said, have a more able or better president than Mr. Pierpoint.—The m.tion was carried by acclamation.—Mr. WM. PIERPOINT, on taking the chair, was enthusiastically cheered. He thanked them very much for tke honour they had just conferred upon him. He felt that having to follow such an able president as they had in the person of their friend, Councillor Fran- comb, he should be placed somewhat at a disadvantage. In the first place, they new Mr. Francorn4 had attained a greater altitude than he had—(laughter)—and on that , account they must expect very much less from him ; but at the same time he thought that most of those who took an interest in football in connection with that club knew

that the club bad bis most earnest sympathies. (Hear, heir.) Whatever he could do for the club he should be pleased to do. (Applause.) There was one thing he should like to say, and that was that heretofore the game had been played in Warrington in a manly, straightforward manner, and he hoped that as they grew in experience and knowledge— for undoubtedly as they grew older they would have better knowledge—they would play football in such a style in Warrington as to be the envy of any club in Yorkshire; and at this point let him say, as their president, bow grati- fied he was to find that matches had b:en arranged with good Yorkshire clubs for next season. He hoped they would be able to render such a good account of theruselvies in the coming season as they bad done in years gone by. (Applause.) He would do all he could to further the in- terests of the club and give it all the support that it was possible for them to expect him to give it. (Applause)

MI CUZZEN DICK. Mi Cuzzen Dick's come hooam ageon, He's left his gallant bark; He wears a nasty ganzey, an His face is rayther dark. He chews thick twist an smooks his pipe, An spits both left an reet ; An when he spins them yarns ov his Truth scutters eawt o' t' sect. Its just a fortnit sin to-day He sed he'd tek a cruise; In his quart kit he packed his clooas, An strapped two bob for booze. Then off he went to t' Bottom Locks, An hedn'd long to wait. Afoor he'd shipped as first mate on Th' owd Wigan frigate" Kate." Aw watched ern sail past Whiteley's Brig, Wind-blown an tempest-tost ; An th' noble captain stood at th' helm, An frothed at meawth an cossed. He sheawted eawt," 0 hands on deck!" Then jumped off wi a whip, An fairly laced th' owd knacker up, As pood his stately ship. Avir lost sect on em at Mill Hill, Then Dick gripped t' steerin pow; An th' captain woked on booard at th' brig, An kicked up sich a row! Past th' Isles o Dogs an Cats they went An fowt to Riley Green: Then th' captain's nooase wurknocked to smash, An Dick hed two black een! Theer t' captain browt a can o ale, An med o reet wi t' mate; Then they ankered to an owd tree stump, For t' fleet wur geddin late. An soon a storm coom teearin on, An waves rolled meawntains high! Tho t' fleet wur wet o th' crew o t' "Kate" • Wur gradely drunk an dry. Neet passed; tort Whittle Springs they went, • • An tupt another ship, Theirs give a lurch to t' leeward side, An then it' cut dud dip. Yet o t' crew bowdly kept ther pooasts, An bawled eawt oer th' uprooar, "If yo wernd come an tek us off, Bigow ! we'll woke ashooare." Fro th' "briney deep" they geet ther booat,— A coyler on th' Can(n)el !-- Wi nod a public-heawse abeawt Ther sufferins—whoa cud tell? They'd no provisions nayther, sooa Fowl thowts they'd nod discard, But nailed a big fat Brama cock, Eawt ov a powltry yard. On th' oppen seea, they've hod to starve,— Three heawrs beawt owt to eyt. Once at a "pub" they'd fourteen pints . Then sloped-0 reck'nins streyt. Sitch tales, he doles eawt to eawr fooak, An preawd they seem to be, Believin every word o Dicks, Bekose he's bin to see! Aw axed him once, while glarin lies He towd at rattlin rate, If Ananias ever wor A gallant booater's mate? "0, ay !" he sed, " aw know her wee!, Hur fells steers t' "Red Moon Aw dosn't ax owl else, bekose He weears big cluntherin shoon. Mi aunt co's him a sailor brave, An eawr fooak fratch an say As he'll command a ship hissel, When ten bob he can pay, At th' booan-heawse, for a "thoro' bred." To pilot him o'er t' fooam ; He wants me to be t' steersmon, but Aw meson to stop at hooam. JACK 0 ANN'S.

div.head: LETTER.
div.p: A LETTER.

A letter was read trout Councillor J H Fleming stating that he regretted not being able to attend that mewing, as be was leaving for a holiday trip. He congratulated the club on the result of last season's work, and hoped that next season would be even better. (Applause.)

div.head: SECRETARY AND TREASURER'S SERVICES.
div.p: THE SECRETARY AND TREASURER'S SERVICES.

The services of the secretary and treasurer were referred to in complimentary terms, and a gratuity of £2O was voted to the treasurer. Mr. Pemberton having acknowledged the gift, a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close. est.

div.head: WARRINGTON_A \TIME QUEEN'
div.p: WARRINGTON- _A \TIME QUEEN'
JUBILEE.

On Monday evening, a meeting of the General Jubilee Committee was held in the Towp Hall, Warrington. The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) presided, and—there was a large attendance. The minutes of the last general meeting, and the two meetings of the Executive Committee, were read.

FRIENDLY SOCIETIW PROCESSION. A letter was read containing a resolution passed at a special district meeting of the Order of Druids in favour of the route of procession. decided upon by the Executive Committee at its meeting on the 20th May. Some discussion then took Place as to the best route for the Friendly Societies' procession. t The representatives of these societies spoke strongly in favour of the route including ns, much of the principal streets as possible. It was ultimately decided that ,the procession should start from the Town Hall, and take the following route: —Arpley- street, Wilson-Patten-street, Bold-street, Sankey- street, Bridge-street, Mersey-street, down Church- Street round the lamp and back up hurch-street, Buttermarket-street, Market Gate, Ibrsemarket- street, Winwick-street, Tanners-lane, Frogliall-lane, , Priestly-street, Bank Quay Bridge, and back to the ' Town Hall. . I TILE SUBSCRIPTIONS AND NUMBER OF SUNDAY I SCHOLARS. . Some talk next took place as to a proposal to give the Friendly Societies .C3O towards the cost of lbands.—Mr. T. JOLLEY said the Finance Committee I would be very pleased to give for bands and fire- works, and to the children and old folks, as much 1 money as they required if they had the money to t give. He was sorry to see that the strong appeal 1 for subscriptions made by the Mayor a week ago i had only resulted in £ll from the 45,000 inhabit- ants. There wasspromised up to date £621 9s, and they had that amount to divide in the best way they possibly could. They might have further sub- scriptions sent in. but if they only increased at the rate of £ll a week that would be only £22. Nearly the whole of the total amount already subscribed , had been subscribed by six persons.—The MAYOR: I imagine there are several hundreds of people waiting till the last week; they are keeping their money till the very last.—Mr. BENNETT fancied there were many people waiting to be called upon. (Hear, hear.)—The MAYOR said it was a question whether or not they should have canvassers. He had advocated that from the first, but several other gentlemen thought that advertising and keeping a list at the banks would be sufficient. For his part he did not think it was, for there were many people who did not care to go to banks to pia their t names down who would be willing no give 2s 6d or i ss.—The Rev. S. WILKINSON said, speaking person- ally for a very large school, that the announcement I that the children were not after all to have 6d per head alllowed them, somewhat staggered him for the simple reason that when that committee was first formed there were three objects decided upon. One was to give the scholars a treat; the, second, to give a dinner to the old folks; the third, to help the arrangements of the Friendly Societies; and the fourth was the scheme for pulling down the wall in front of the Town Hall if means were ; forthcoming. He thought they might safely say that the fourth object would never be carried out because sufficient funds were not coming in. (Hear, hear.) But with regard to the schools, they be- lieved they would get their 6d per head from that fund, and they had consequently not yet collected one farthing,and he thought many other schools had not collected a farthing. If they did not get their six- pences, therefore, many of them would have to put their hands in their own pockets and make up the , amount required. Speaking for their own schools, , he might safely say that it was now too late to com- mence collecting. (Hear, hear.) There was another thing a good deal had been said about, and that was the large number of Sunday scholars that were sup- posed to exist inWarrington. He believed that a great number of them thought before the numbers ac- tually came in that 10,000 would be about the number but instead of 10,000 the returns amounted to about 13,500. There were certain people who thought 1 that number too great. These people might be. right, or they might be wrong. ("Wrong.") Well, he was not quite so sure about that, but he thought that figures could be given to show that the figures sent in were not so very far wrong, and Sunday sesool teachers would not willingly, send in false numbers. (Hear, hear.) He knew that theirl teachers were men of the highest respectability, I and they had gone most carefully into the matter to I see that their figures were correct.' There was a suggestion that some children's names appeared, perhaps, on two or three registers, and they knew that within the last few weeks a new school had I been started—and all honour to those gentlemen I who started it—he meant the Ragged School in Bewsey-street, and some of the children who at- tended there might also have their names on other Sunday school registers. Mr. Wilkinson then sug- gested that by means of tickets the number of children that was provided for by each school could be ascertained. The scholar, he pointed out, whose name was on two or three-registers could only par- take of the treat of one school. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. F. MONKS tben read the estimate of expenditure formed by the committee. They estimated for ad- vertising, printing, postages, &c., £lOO. (" Oh, oh.") They had set down .£3O for the friendly societies, but they wanted more, and the estimate had been raised to £5O. The old folks' treat was down for £75, and they would not provide fireworks for much less than £lOO. ("Oh, yes.") For contingencies there was £75. (It Voice: What are they?) Well, if they had fireworks they would want barricading, and there were a number of other expenses which they knew would be incurred. If they in addition estimated for 10,000 children at 6d per head, that would be £250, and if they added the whole up together they would find it was £650, while up to then the subscriptions amounted only to £621. If the number of children that had been returned were paid for at Gd per head, it practically ran away with half of the whole fund. He confessed he was still one of those that could scarcely believe that there are 13,500 children in the Sunday schools in Warrington. In 1873, at the open- ing of Bank Hall, there were 7,594 children paid for, and it required some imagination to credit that the number had risen so largely since then.—A. REPRESENTATIVE said that the 1873 returns did not include the Roman Catholic children.—Mr. Mimics said that he had no doubt that on the whole the re- turns were accurrate, but they had it on. pretty good authority that some schools could not accom- -1 modate the numbers returned.—lt was mentioned that the Salvation Amu/ children would not be present in 1873, and in answer to Mr. Monks it was stated that the number returned by the Army was 1 790.—The REPRESEN'ATIVE of the Salvation Army suggested that their, children might be counted as they entered the field.—Mr. MONKS remarked that that raised the question as to whether they were to treat the whole of the children of the town or only the Sunday school children. He did not hesitate to say that he did not believe there were 13,500

CHAPTER L AN Trani BELLIC.:'!AriII Heaven bless thee! Thou bast the sweetest face I ever Inolted on. N'taksplfre. "Tracy, my dearest of cousins, what do you think happened last night ?" This was a strange greeting, but. then Hyacinth Des- mond and Tracy Mansfield had known each other for years—long enough to have quarrelled when she was in 'pinafores and he in round jackets; and they Saw each other almost daily, for Tracy lived with his mother and Lister in the "big house". yonder, not two miles from the e welling of Mrs. ind Mia. 3 Desmond, so formal greetings were as often as not dispensed with. , The Scene was a bit of wild common, land in county Galway, and the person addressed ,by .14iss Hyacinth Desmond as cousin was a good-looking young Irishman , of about twenty-four, who, although the cut of his kothes would not have passed muster itfrall Mall, was .7.ertainly a gentleman and well born; and, indeed,'Mr. Tracy Mansfield was the Lovelace of the region round zbout Curramore, .and as the possessor of a tolerable ',state, and some money in the funds besides, he was a very eligible para. r.i Hyacinth Desmond; seated on her shaggy pony; would. have formed a pbrfect Picture, with the rugged back,' ground of heath and hill and wood; and very likely Tracy Mansfield—though he was not particularly rementic—thought so. She was a- tall, slim girl of eighteen, with that free grace of bearing and movement that shows untrammelled exorcise of the limbs—a most beautiful girl, too, with large 'flashing black eyes, fault- lessly cut lips—very firm and proud were those lips- 4nd curly masses of dark chestnut hair, which rolled anti tumbled bewitchingly over her small shapely bead. She was riding without a 'riding habit, and in her race over the common her broad hat .had fallen MI and dangled ,iehind her; therich glow of exercise mantled over her `soft brickdust skin and her, .4 wild dark eyes" were Apatkling with fun, as pulling up her pony with a prac- tised jerk, she called out the above-recorded question with her riveetTrish 'voice and dainty brogue. . "A kiss first, Hyacinth," Tracy answered, laying his on She:wines untrimmed' mane, 44 before I ask, you ' what you mean."'

"Vary well," said she, bending down, and receiving toe kiss in cousinly, matter-of-course fashion. "Now, don't you want to know ?" "How can I guess? Moll Grady's spotted cow has run away, or Terence O'Conor is back from the Cur- ragh— " You're burning," cried Tiya.cinth, clappin,.; icier pretty hands. " Curra—Curra—Curramore—" "Something happened at Curramore, do you mean ? What can happen there ?" "You dolt! You might be a Saxon yourself to be so slow. Why, Vincent Lorraine • opped down like Mephistopheles himself on Curramore last night. Isn't that news ?" "Vincent Lorraine!" repeated Mansfield, falling bark .1 step. "What in the world brings him down here? You are joking, Hyacinth !" "I never was more serious in my life. Nobody ex- pected him. Dolly Maguire told me, and old Margaret Finnigan told her, and it was just this way," Hyacinth went on, with that instinct of her people Sin. dramatic narrative. "It was half-past ten by the clock, and Mar- garet was just going up to bed, when a loud ring came t the bell: Up she jumps, 'all of a thrinable,' and blesses ,nerself, and mutters,' Holy Vargin,presarye us,' thinking banshee at least is outside; and white she is so engaged !!le ring comes again, and Margaret, thinking it must be •i human being—or the Evil Oise—runs up to the great loor, and looks through the little window by it, and :creams out Whose there!' ait,t rile answer comes back, 'Vincent Lorraine '—and Vincent Lorraine it was. He cad come, goodness knows how, but without a note of warning, and," said Hyacinth, solemnly, "I have it on the authority of Dolly Maguire, v..ho had it from Mar- garet Finnigan, that this same Vincent Lorraine is 'the very handsomest gentleman' she (Margaret) iver sot 'yes on.' So mind your p's and q's, Tracy, for you know chat a dangerous fellow Lorraine is." " Cromwell's curse on him!" said young Mansfield. ' tell you what, Hyacinth; 'tis those Gradys that have brought him; he would be just the kind of man tc take the bull by the horns ; but it won't do—he'll get, shot for his pains." .. . .

"Tracy, do you think its that ? Do you think be is bent on ejecting Grady?" "It looks like it; and I hope Lorraine may win the day, that's all! What did old I,,orraine buy the property for? He had great estates in England—nobody wanted a Saxon landlord for Curramore ; and the estate isn't worth £l,OOO a year at its best. Old Lorraine has been here twice in the ten years since he bought it, and Vin- cent, though his father died three years ago, has not nice. He'll try and carry things with a high hand, anC. I said, get shot." "Still," observed Hyacinth, a thoughtful shade setting m her broad brow, "matters at Currarnore need some tooking after; the Gradys are the worst of all the tenants. and corrupt the others; but they are all behindhand with the rent; the Grady's haven't paid for two years, and Dermot boasts that he can pay, but 'isn't going to pay to a young prolligit." "I can't altogether blame him, Hyacinth. Rumour may exaggerate, but it's right in the main, and you know what it says of Vincent Lorraine. Besides, didn't Terence O'Conor tell us that when he was in London Lorraine had the reputation of one of the fastest men in town? He's immensely rich, and what does he do with his mosey? Keeps a. racing stud, drives four-in-hand, gambles, and goes the pace generally; and these poor farmers are to grind their lives out to pay rents that my Lord would squander in dissipation." " said Hyacintl-.., stroking her pony's neck. however bad he is, his tenants ought to pay their rents; but he's foolish to try the high-handed policy. I sun. pose Murphy has given up the matter as a had job ?" 'He has; at least he told me a week ago that he had written to Lorraine and tcld hilt he could do no more-t. that his life had been twice threatened already; so I suspect it is his letter which has brought Lorraine over, and he thinks, no doubt, that he'll conquer as his Norman ancestors did." -

"I admire his pluck," said Hyacinth, laughing "but it's no laughing matter. He cannot know what! he is undertaking." "I hope he will find out, and depart as quickly as he came," said Mansfield, aunost savagely, "for he is no acquisition; his way of living doesn't suit our notions, and if he is up to any of his games he may get. a bullet through him before he has a chance to ask for his a rents."

"He isn't as bad as you say, sure," said Hyacinth, looking shocked. "All you know, Hyacinth. I heard things of him from, O'Conor that I couldn't tell to you. He's a thorough vil- lain; and if he's good-looking, so much the worse. Scamps like him usually have handsome faces toAnake fools think that handsome does because handsome is."

"It wouldn't make me think so," said Hyacinth, shaking her curls. "I don't like scamps. As for horse-racing, he will be puzzled to pursue that amusement hpre, and he couldn't play cards with old Margaret. I wonder if he means to content himself with her so/us for a servant— he has not even brought his valet with him. I tho Ight such a 'swell' could not dress himself without the aid of a valet " "Oh, these exquisites can help themselves fast enough when they choose !" said Tracy. " Ikalf their dandy ways are affectation. Lorraine, evidently, has no small allowance of the buccaneet in his disposition, though I suppose he has lily hands and wears diamond studs and rings, and wouldn't believe himself clothed if any one but the first tailor in town made for him." Hyacinth laughed. " Well," said she, "I must be off, for I have to be out and home in two hours. I promised mother I would be back to tea. I shall come over to Durmabog to-morrow. Good-bye, coz." And away she trntted, Tracy Mansfield watching her as long as she was in sight. I am afraid he was thipking, more about his cousin than she was thinking of him just now. She was very fond of him, but not at all in love with him, and as she rode across the wild heath and along the lane beyond, her head was running on the complications she foresaw between Vincent Lorraine and his tenants. Clearly, she argued, he did not understand Irish peasants; but then, though an Irish girl, Hyacinth Desmond was painfully sensible of the fact that it was no easy task for anyone to understand the ignorant classes of her countrymen. She was going to make a few purchases in the little village of Ballygoyle, which was more than two miles from her home, and her way lay across a potato field, which was a'short cut to her destination. As she drew near to the gate of this field she heard the sound •of a man's voice, and slackening her speed, she recognised the tones of Dan Murphy, the Curramore agent, a man hateq simply because lie was a laud-agent, but in reality kind- hearted and faithful in his work. "Who is he talking to, I wonder," thought Hyacinth. The next moment she turned a corner, and came in full view of the gate and those who stood by it. There was Dan Murphy, his knobley stick under his arm, his hat Very much on one side, as was proper for an Irishman, talking volubly to a young man who, leaning with careless, unstudied grace of attitude against the gate, seemed to be listening half-contemp- tuously to the agent's tale. In this young man Hyacinth did not doubt she beheld Mr. Vincent Lorraine himself. tie was tall, slender, fashionably dressed—aristocrat

div.head: 'ED • I
div.p: 'ED • I

from crown to heel—with a lace that more than! endorsed old Margaret's opinion, for its beauty was so! striking that the least observant person must notice it. Details Hyacinth could not yet see, beyond these—that the features were cut with exceeding delicacy, the com- plexion dark and very pale, and the hair and moustache ' 1--he wore neither beard nor whiskers—of a dark chest- .'nut colour. Furthermore, Hyacinth thought that his beauty would lose nothing by a less haughty expression. So much she bad seen—and it occupied only a moment —when she was herself perceived, first by Mr. Lorraine, who suddenly lifted his eyes, and fixed on the lovely equestrian a look of such undisguised admiration that, little vain as Hyacinth was, the bold keen gaze made her colour rise and her own eyes droop. Murplo,turned round quickly, in the same instant, and with a quiek— " Arrah, now, pardon, soiri—'tis Miss Hyacinth De* inond-==bleas her !" sprang to the pony's side, :touching his hat with respectful familiarity, adding, "An' are ye goin' to Ballygoyle, missy ?" "Yea; and I was only to be two hours out and home" returned Hyacinth, painfully conscious that those hand- some brilliant eyes of Vincent Lorraine were watching her, though he had withdrawn his first admiring glance with a slight smile when he saw the colour mount to her cheek. ' .

"Then you'll be going this way, missy ?" pointing I towards the field; and Hyacinth had half a :mind to i make up some reason for going straight on. so as to avoid pologies or thanks to that haughty young Englishman, tt.• whom, despite his beauty, she had taken a decided, and not unnatural, dislike. It was too late, however; for Vincent Lorraine, seeing Murphy's gesture . turned ,to Hyacinth, his hat and bowing with a courtly grace that almost Condoned his offence, and addressed her in one.of those flute-like voices that are dangerous weapons in the possession of unscrupulous fnen. "Am I obstructing your path, Miss Desmond. Ibe your pardon." " Don't apologise, please." said Hyacinth, with her sunny Irish smile. "I have no exact right to cross that field, only it is a short cut, and the owner allows me to trespass." 'Happy owner, and happy land," said Lorraine, laying on the gate a delicate, beautifully-formed hand, as smooth and as whitens a woman's, and looking up into the, girl's winsome face with a look that too clearly pointed the words; but. sh 6 'hardly coloured at all this time gazed straight beck at him with a very de- cided frownybutshe did not succeed in upsetting M. I Lorraine'i equanimity: he lowered his eyes certainly, but "smiled again rather provokingly, as it. Hyacinth's rebuff amused him as a child's coquetry might have done, ,and added coolly, slowly opening the gate the while. "If the land were timly mine, Miss Desmond, you might ride straight over the crops, and I should feel 1 honoured," 1 Hyacinth thought he spoke ironically; his face—the moment she saw it—she.wed her that he was given to ' sarcasm, and she felt very indignant that after the reproof he had received he should laugh at her and add another and. more extravagant compliment. "I suppose the land is yours,". she said at once, "it (lid belong to Mick Rooney, who has not paid his rent, and is under notice to quit" . , . I did not know this was Mick Rooney's land. But I meant what I said, only 1. suppose it :Rooney saw you riding over the crops he would shoot you, would he not?" . . , .

Och, Tlisther LorrainC t.'!'cried Murphy, holding up his hands: but Hyacinth said, "You wouldn't think it a sin and shame to ride doWn a poor man's crops ?" Well, yes: but! ain not a poor man, Miss Desmond, and you have just told me that the crops are mine." "Not yours to destroy." "A man, then, may not do as he will With his own?" He asked the questions as if Hyacintlf s„proposition 'enclosed a dobtrine quite new to him,"—is Very likely it %.-as ("selfish spaipeon !" see thought to herWf) ; yet she could not be sure that he 'ipoke Sitterely. She chose, however, to treat the remark as genuine, in order to give him a rap.

" Maybe you think. so," she said, "but I'd be sorry to help vou in carrying out vour ideas." " What are yours?" asked Lorraine, just a trifle mock. i ugly. "The general :Irish' View, you know, seems to .be that, from doing what he Will with hi own, a man's knd is, not his own' but belongs—to 'make a bull '—to somoixidr.else, and that he is a tyrant if he asks for his rents. Do you share these—to tile—odd opinions ?" Be was lightly stroking Shemus's mane while he spoke, with that lily" hand *domed with rings that rent up dazzling rays firefin'llathing brilliants; and she glanced at the hand with a more than ordinary interest, and from that to its owner's face. She could not help rscalling the courtier-soldiers of mediieval Italy of whom she had read, who seemed too. delicately made for sterner stuff than lounging in ladies' bowers' whose locks were perfumed, and their fingers jewelled, wild who yet were crafty and ruthless in statecraft, cruel and relentless in oattle, with wills of iron, and the Steel grasp ever hidden in the velvet glove. She was not surprised -now that soft-voiced, white-banded Vincent Lorraine had come to this wild place to set his heel .on rebellion. She could fancy him quite ruthless where he was determined to conquer--,a man whose passions might sweep him to destruction, but whose will could control even those passions if he chose to exert it—tt man with regard to whom no medium position was possible. You might hate him, or love him, but lukewarm affection or in- difference was out of the question. . . . . . _
- • Thought is quick enough to cover a great deal of ground in half a moment, and it was no more than that before Hyacinth answered her interlocutor.

"No, don't share these opinions, and they are drily held here by ignorant people. 'Tis sorry lam that any shcluld hold them, and bring reproach on the country; but the prejudice is too strong to be rooted out:" . . . .

. . ls it ?'Mid he, with a !oar the, girl liked less than his curiously intent manner of gazing at her; "then thy tenants, Miss Desmond, will have to pay dearly fortheir prejudices. I mean to be master !"

. - "Ah, sorr." here interposed Murphy, "it's madness— they'll shoot ye—they will indade.' Lorraine half smiled. "I am a dead shot," he said, "and not, very scrupulous." No need to say it—he looked it; and yet his hand was t ray in g over the pony's mane RS tenderly and as cares- singly as a mother might touch a sick child. Hyacinth thought of the tenants—poor and ragged, some of them--and the worth of a single stone in one of the rings this man wore, would more than buy up the whole of a farm; yet, after all, the land was his. But it was not pleasant to hear a man who held so lightly by the obligations of property talk so ruthlessly of enfor- cing his own rights. Of course it was not the money he cared for ; but he ought to be more tolerant of ignor- ance, more mindful of the fact that he, living for his own pleasure, was really as oblivious of his duties with regard to property as his Irish tenants. "Some of these people," the girl said, "are less scru- pulous than you are, Mr. Lorraine, and would not give you a chance for a shot. Good-evening. I shall be late home if lam not off. Good evening, Dan Murphy." "Good evening, missy. God bless ye !" "You must go ?" said Lorraine's flute-like voice, "but I hope I shall have the pleasure of meeting, you again. Good evening.'. _ _ _

He did not-, of course, offer his hand, but Hyacinth would have offered hers if he had not looked at her again with not only unmistakable admiration, but something more in the dark gray, eyes which said almost as "We shall meet again." So she only said once more, rather coldly, "Good evening," and rode away across the potatoe-field.

Lorraine watched her for several minutes in 'a silence which Murphy did not like. to interrupt; then turning round, the young master of Curramore asked nonchal- antly.— " Who is Miss Hyacinth Desmond?"

" The Desmondi are wan of the ouldest families in Oireland, yer anner; there's little enough money, but the good blood is the thing.. Miss Hyacinth lives with her mother, over beyond the common. It's the swatest young lady as ever was, she is, an' the purtiest." " Pretty !" said Vincent Lorraine to himself, "the most witching face eyes ever rested on !" but aloud, " Yes ; she's awfully good-looking. We had better go on a bit now, Murphy.' "Very well, yer anner. They do say," continued the agent, pushing his hat still more on one side, "that Misther Tracy Mansfield—that's Miss Hyacinth's cousin --is swate on her, and they'd make a good match, I should say." "Ah !" said Lorraine. indifferently; "do you smoke cigarettes, Murphy ?"'drawing out the daintiest of cases, embroidered, evidently by a female hand. "Faith, sorr," said Dan, laughing, "they're too grand for the likes o' me—flyer smoked wan in my loife." "They have no taste, maybe," said Lorraine, laughing, too. "Well, then, light up a pipe if you prefer it—no ceremony." Thus adjured, Murphy drew forth a "clay," and Lor- raine, lighting his cigarette, added, "Look you, Murphy, Dermot Grady has had his last chance. lam going to him to-morrow to serve a final notice with my own hand." "Oh, yer anner—" "Fool,, pooh! When I make up my mind, my friend, not even a woman could turn me aside—and that is say- ing a great deal. So no more words, lam going—and I go alone. I know from you row who can pay and who cannot. Let those who cannot ask mercy, and they shall have it; but if every rood of this land goes to waste, no man shall live on it or till it who denies my rights and defies me. They may shoot me, but they will flat frighten me.' And Dan Murphy was silent. Clearly Mr. Vincent Lorraine was not to be trifled with. CM be continued.) • ;, ,

PAT'S DEFENCE.—A soldier of a cavalry regiment during the Crimean war was brought up for stealing his com- rade's liquor-ration. He was an Irishman, and his de- fence was unique: "I'd be sorry indade, sur, to be called a thief. I put the liquor in the same bottle, and mine i was at the bottom, and shure I was obliged to drink his to get at my own. Och, sur, it's meself that'd scorn to be a thief !"

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
ROUSE OF COMMONS.--Mortitty.
The House re-assembled after the Whitsuntide recess, and the Speaker took the chair at 3 50 p.m.
QUESTIONS.

The LORD ADVOCATE, in reply to Mr. Fergtisson, said It was intended by the Government to introduce in the House of Lords, on an early day, a bill completing the powers of the Secretary for Scotland. Mr. DOCON-HARTLARD frilled the First Lord of the Treasury whether, in view of the lamentable accident at the Opera Comique in Paris, and the fact that such an accident might occur in London at any time, in con- sequence of the non-inspection of theatres, he would allow his (Mr. Dixon-Hartland's) bill, which stood for second rending on Wednesday next, to take precedence of the Crimes Bill. Mr. W. H. SMITH said it was not in his power to accede to the desire of the hon. gentleman. Replying to Mr. A. O'Connor, the flows SECRETARY said that one of the inspectors of mines and a Scotch barrister would conduct an inquiry into the disaster which had occurred at the Udston Colliery. He was afraid that he had no means at his disposal to reward the heroism displayed by the rescue party. Sir J. GORST, in reply to Mr. Bradlaugh, said the Secretary for India was not in possession of such offi- cial information as was requisite to enable him to answer the detailed inquiries of the hon. gentleman regarding the leasing of the Ruby Mines in Blimp, but he had referred to India for full information.

SUPPLY.—PATTERN POST. The House then went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates.—The vote for the Post Office was taken first, and gave rise to a long discussion. —Mr. BRADLAUGH criticised the general system on which the patronage of the Postmaster-General is ex- ercised, and brought forward a number of instances in which he contended the ordinary, course had been de- parted from. Mr. Hartmxan HEATON suggested various reforms, such as telegraphic money orders, a penny postage rate to the colonies, &c. Mr. RAtxEs, in replying, said the hon. member for Canterbury had raised the question of telegraphic money orders, and although there were advantages in the system so far as convenience was concerned, there was a very great risk in largely increasing the balances to be deposited in the hands of the provincial post- masters. He had given the matter some consideration, but he had not been able to get over that obstacle. There had not been any great demand on the part of the public for these orders. If there had been the difficulty might have been overcome. But at present there was no sufficient reason to introduce the system. One statement, however, the committee wonld be glad to hear, viz., that within the last few days he had obtained the sanction of the Treasury to the re-establishment of a pattern post. Be did not propose to go beyond a weight allowance of half a pound at present, and he proposed a graduated system so. that any sample or pattern weighing less than 4oz. should be conveyed for id., between 4oz. and 6oz. lid., and between Boz. and Boz. 2d. He believed this would fully meet the exigencies of the case, and would get rid of the grave scandal of patterns being sent to the Con- tinent, and then re-transmitted to this country, this country getting no part of the revenue, of course. It was only intended that this post should cover bond Po samples and patterns, and not be Used as a means of defrauding the revenue by sending letters at a cheap rate. Dr. CAMERON regretted that instead of establishing a pattern post the minimum of the parcel post had not been reduced. Our postal rates had become too compli- cated, and should be simplified instead of increased. Mr. SHAW-LEFEVER suggested that, as the difficulty in making improvements generally arose with the Treasury, there should be an understanding that only a certain portion of the profits of the Post Office—say £3,000,000 —should be appropriated for revenue purposes, and that the remainder should be devoted to improvements. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHIMVEH pointed out that the profits earned bythe departmentwere mainlyderived from the great bulk of the community—the penny letter writers,—and they ought to have the benefit of the pro- fits, for he thought it would be manifestly unfair to use these profits for extending or improving another branch of the business of the department. But if it could be shown that a lower rate for colonial postage could be made to pay, the Treasury would be glad to second any reform in this direction which the Post Office might Mr. PICKERSGILL complained of the charge for medical substitutes, and moved the reduction of the vote by £lOO. This was negatived on a division by 111 to 31, and after some further conversation the vote was agreed to, as was also the vote for the Post Office Packet Service.

div.head: TELEGRAPHS.
div.p: THE TELEGRAPHS.

On the Telegraph vote of £1,500,248, a brief discussion as to arrangements with railway companies for way- leaves and maintenance, &c., was raised by Dr. CAMERON, who moved a reduction of the vote ; but this was nega- tived by 132 to 60. . Subsequently Mr. RAMER, in response to an appeal from Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, went at length into the tele- graph accounts, the expenditure on works, the working expenses generally, and the revenue, the result being that since 1880-81 a surplus of £313.000 of revenue over working expenses had been converted into a deficit of £223,000, which, added to the £326,000 interest on the capital cost of the telegraphs, showed a total deficit this year of £s3o,ooo.—The vote was then agreed to. MISCELL A NEO US. On the motion for the second reading of the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill, Sir W. HARCOURT commented on the proposal to reduce the sinking fund, which he viewed with alarm and regret, and contended that it was contrary to all prece- dent and altogether•opposed to the principles of sound finance. Mr. BARTLEY referred to the growing increase of ex- penditure in the Civil departments, with which he thought the Budget failed to deal adequately. 4 The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER recognised the danger of allowing the local debt to increase, but pointed cut that it was not touched by the Budget. As to the increase in the expenditure he remarked that he had not the same control over the Estimates as he had over the revenue; and, answering the objections to the pro- posed reduction of the Sinking Eiind, he failed to see that it would adversely affect future financial proposals. The bill was then read a second time, as was 'Ad the National Debt and Local Loans Bill. _ _ .
The Committee on Army and Navy Estimates, consist- ing of 19 members, was appointed on the motion of Mr. W. H. SMITH; and the House adjoarned at 1 50 a.m.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. NOTICE.—Mr. STANLEY LEIGHTON gave notice that in a fortnight he will move that the House, while prepared to give a general support to her Majesty's Government in the management of public business, is of opinion that, too much time having been already spent in its consideration, the Crimps Bill should be passed through its remaining stages in a short and limited period.—The CHIEF SECRETARY was asked by Mil Crilly whether it was a fact that the gunboat Banterer had been ordered to assist in carrying out evictions in Clare Island and Clare Bay, and if it was the intention of the Government to bring in the assistance of the naval forces to aid the soldiers and the police who are engaged in carrying out evictions in Ireland.—Mr. BALFOUR replied that it was not improbable that tbe fads were as stated, and that the Government would not hesitate in case of necessity to employ any forces at their disposal to carry out decrees of the courts of law. THE COERCION BILL.

The House again went into Committee on the Crimes Bill, and at the outset Mr. BALFOUR desired to follow the ex- ample set by the First Lord of the Treasury the other day, and make a statement "for the benefit of those who had , not gone through the amendments on the psper," but objec- tion was taken by Mr. Labonchere, Mr. Healy, and other , members, and the statement was not made.—The discussion of the bill was then resumed at clause 3. Sir W. HARCOURT. , in recommending the withdrawal of an amendmentouggested they should discuss only amendments that raised vital that points in the clause, and divide against the clause as a pro- teat against the principle of the bill generally.—Mr. PAR- NELL t bought this was good advice.—Mr. A. 0 Comm moved to except treason-felony or treason from the opera- tion øf the clause, but it was negatived by a majority of 73. —Mr. WARTRuit moved an amendment specifying the crimea to be dealt with under the clause.—lt was rejected by 203 to 117.—A proposal made by Mr. T. EIEALY that where then) was a special jury there should be no change of venue was rejected by 153 to 84 ; and an amendment moved by Mr M. Healey that tbe clause should not apply to I cases to be tried in the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court was defeated by 137 to 67. Other amendments i were dispesed of in a similar manner. In the case of an j amendment moved by Mr. T. Healey to omit the provision I empowering a defendant te apply for a special jury—which, Ibe said, was designed in the interest of a special and abominable class of offenders—the closure was moved by Mr. Smith, and was carried by 229 against 98. This was followed by a proposal by Mr. Smith that the clause stand part of the bill, his object being to shut out 27 amendments on the paper; but the Chairman refused to allow the quest- , tion to be put, on the ground that there were two or three provisons which deserved some debate. HOUSE OF COMMONS.-z-WEDNEsDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes after twelve o'clock. THE COERCION BILL—The consideration of the Irish Crimps Bill was resumed at clause 4, which provides for a change f venue.—Mr. T. M. limr moved to omit the preamble of the clause, but Mr. BALFoun objected.--Mr. J. MORLEY thought this refusal was au excellent illustration of what was meant when they charged upon want of com- petency in those who conducted the bill the responsibility for the delay which had taken place. The Government must have linown that to insert this preamble was sure to provoke members below the gangway to dispute and chal- lenge it, as it was a pure piece of provocation and added nothing to the strength of the bill. Having said this, he recommended the mover of the amendment to proceed to a division without further debate.—Sir W. Lawson insisted that the great obstructer of the bill was the Chief Secretary. —Upon a division the amendment was negatived by 180 to 116. Progress was then reported, and the House adjourned at six o'clock.
HOUSE OF LOEDS.—Txuasney. Tbe Lord Chancellor took his seat at twenty minutes after four o'clock, this being the first meeting of their Lord..

RACE-LOTTERY PROSECUTIONS.—TWO lottery proseca- tions came before the North Shields magistrates on Mon. day. Robert Mould, landlord of the Marquis of Lorne Inn, and Thomas Melville, landlord of the Saddle Inn, were charged with selling lottery tickets. Evidence was given with respect to Ole purchase of lottery tickets, having reference to horse races pending. The magis- trates considered the cases proved, and fined the defend- ants in the mitigated penalty of 40s. and costs in each Case. GOVERNMENT SERVANTS AND CONTRACTS.—An important notification, has been issued by the Secretary of War to the various branches of the War Office and its manufac- turing departments, to the effect that the practice of qfficials holding shares or being interested in companies which contract with the Government is highly detri- mental to the public service, and must be abandoned; in fact, that in future any official of' the War Office or ita departments who shall bold any such shares will be liable to dismissal. Yublic Analysts have submitted CADnuinee CoCOA to Close tests, and the result has always proved its great value Fw a sus- taining aed nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— y der.

It is stated that the Queen has promised to distribute, this year, the prizes and certificates awarded by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. A farewell banquet was given in New York on Tuesday night to Mr. O'Brien, and in the course of the proceedings a sum of £5,000 was banded to him for Mr. Parnell from the Parliamentary Fund Association. The new twin screw belted cruiser Immortalit6 was launched at Chatham on Tuesday. Her arsnour belt is 10 inches thick She is of 5,000 tons displacement, 8,500 horse- power, and with an estimated speed of 18 knots. MURDER OF CHILDREN IN LIVERPOOL—On Tuesday, a woman named Armstrong, wife of a seaman in the employ of the Cunard Co., and residing in Kirkdaie, a suburb of Liverpool, murdered two of her children, and so. badly in- jured a third that it is not expected to tecover. She smothered one child, and cut the throats of the other two. They were aged ten months, two years, and three years. The woman is believed to be demented.

• SHOCKING CHARGE AGAINST A GIRL At Lam beth Police Court, on Tuesday, Jane Bruce, a girl of z•ixteen years, was charged With procuring young girls, and Mary Bennett, Edward Prockuell, and Esther .Procknell were charged with allowing these girls to be on their premises for unlawful purposes. The case was of a most shocking character. One of the victims was a child of ten, and two others, aged thirteen, gave evidence in support of tha charges. The prisoners were remanded. Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength ii unequalled.--Advf,

ships after the adjournment for the Whitsuntide holidays on the 23rd May.—Several private bills were read a third time and passed. Their lordships adjourned at twenty•five minutes to five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tatmsney.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. , The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER stated that the greater portion of the £50,000 to be granted for public works in Ireland would be devoted to arterial drainage, and it was the intention of the Government to undertake at once the surveys recommended by the Royal Commission as a preliminary to the establishment of Conservancy Boards for the execution of drainage works in the several river basins. —The PosTstesTga GENERAL stated that on Jubilee day the arrangements would be such as would afford postal and telegraph officials as much relief as possible. In the country there would be for the most part one delivery and sue col- lection of letters and parcels, and rural postmen after corn- pleting their delivery would be allowed to return at once to their starting points, as on Christmas Day. In the metro- polis there will be one early and one late delivery, and corresponding collections, and one delivery and ens collec- tion of parcels. " QUIBBLE." - Colonel King-Harman, the Assistant Secretary, was required to explain the terms upon which the Royal Irish Constabulary have been called upon to con- tribute to a Jubilee fund. The Colonel's answer drew from Mr. T. Healy the comment that one previously given on the same subject by Mr. Balfour must have been "some. what of a quibble.' Upon hearing this remark the Speaker loudly cried "Order," and requested Mr. Healy to withdraw the word. This was done after some pressure, and a little scene.
MR. GLADSTONE IN WALES.-GREAT NATIONAL DEMONSTRATION.-IMPORTANT SPEECHES ON THE IRISH QUESTION.

IA monster Liberal demonstration took place in the grounds of Singleton Abbey, Swansea, the seat of Si; Hussey Vivian, on . Saturday afternoon. Excursionists from all parts of the Principality arrived, no fewer than sixty special trains being on the rails in addition to the ordinary service. All works were closed, and the day was observed as a general holiday. Upwasds of 100,000 persons • were expected to take part in the march-past before the ex-Premier, and it is estimated that fully that number were present. Tile Irish deputations from Cork and Waterford arrived at Milford Haven in the morning, and proceeded to Singleton Abbey, where, with the other numerous deputations, they presented an ad- dress to Mr. Gladstone, accompanied with a gold hurly pendant, or real Irish polished MIME& and ball. A deptltation from the Welsh Nonconformist ministers also waited upon the right hon. gentleman. The large body of processionists, wearing green and white rosettes, and many of them bearing banners of the same colours, mustered at two rendezvous and marched six deep to Singleton. At twelve o'clock the first contingent of the procession arrived at the gates of the park, and at the same moment Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone came out of the house, and took up the central position to receive their visitors. With them were the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, Sir Hussey and Lady Vivian, Lord Aberdare, Lord Ken- sington, and a number of M.P.'s. Mr. Gladstone was loudly cheered, and cries were raised tor "Home Rule for Ireland" and "Home Rule for Wales."

Mr. GLADSTONE said they had witnessed a wonderful and affecting sight. (dheers.) Let him select for com- mendation one banner upon which was written in words of eloquence and truth, "Union of hearts, not of man- acles." The hearts of the people were moved because they were met on an occasion which wap Imperial, Irish, and Welsh. (Hear, hear.) It was Imperial because the character and honour of the empire required that an end should be put to the painful relations between England and Ireland, which for cmturies had shocked the feel- ings and the judgment of the whole civilised world. It was Irish because Ireland had the deepest interest in their proceedings, inasmuch as the object was to restore the basis of social order, and to bring the feelings of the people into harmony with the action of the law. (Cheers.) It *as also a Welsh occasion. He could not express the satisfaction with which he observed the firm determina- tion of Protestant Wales to do justice, and nothing less than full justice, to Roman Catholic Ireland. (Cheers.) Referring to the nationality of Wales, he said although they were a distinct nationality, that did not mean they were disunited from England. It meant a closer union with England. (Cheers.) The recognition of the distinctive qualities of the separate parts of great countries and empires constituted the true basis of union, and the attempt to centralise them by destroy- ing their local peculiarities was the shallowest philosophy and the worst possible of all practical blunders. (Cheers.) Ile was not going to compare the grievances—or, as it was better to call them, the inconveniences—of Wales with tiCe grievances of Ireland. He was not going to compare the history of the relations between England and Wales with the deplorable, disgraceful, shocking, and revolting history—(hear, hear)—of the relations between England and Ireland. Anxious as he was to put an end to the sorrows of Ireland, he was more anxious to live to see the day when the deepest stain that lay on the Eng- lish character and reputation should be removed by the final work of doing justice to Irish grievances. (Cheers.) The inconveniences of Wales had received insufficient attention, because she had been too patient and too silent. (Hear, hear.) It was time that their representa- tives should in moderation, and subject to the claims of Imperial patriotism, lay their heads together and con- sider what were the fair claims of Wales. Many of them were anxious to deal with the question of Disestabliahment. (Cheers.) He meant to do nothing except to give his adhesioTh to what he called the Hartingtonian principle. When Lord Hartington was leading the Liberal party in the time of the Beaconsfield Ministry he went into Scot- land for a more useful purpose than he had recently done, and in reply to a question Lord Hartington said that the question whether there should continue to be an Established Church in, Scotland ought to be settled according to the views and Convictions of the Scotch. That was the Hartingtonian principle, and he was a thorough Hartingtonian in its adoption. (Laughter and cheers.) In England, Scotland, or Wales, it was accord- ing to the views of the people that the matter should be decided. (Cheers.) There were many other things. There was the tithe question. He had read with regret the proceedings in connection with the collection of tithes in North Walea. All he had to say was—Firstin one respect he was glad that these disturbances were in Wales and not in Ireland, because, if they were in Ireland, they would immediately introduce a new Coercion Bill— (laughter); and, secondly, they illustrated his position. Welsh questions which were urgent could not be discussed in consequence of the state of business in Parliament There were gentlemen of imaginations so keen as to say that he was the man who had caused Ireland to have the baneful, deplorable, and grievous monopoly of the time of Parliament. That was fundamentally untrue. (Cheers.) Ireland used her power to return 86 National members out of 101. and until the great and fundamental sore of Ireland could be healed that wound was so griev- ous and deep that the Irish question, in one shape and another, must tie the primary, cardinal, and absorbing subject of the deliberation of Parliament Last year the late Government took up the time of Parliament with the discussion of Home Rule. This year the present Government had taken up all the time of the House of • Commons even all private members' nights —in devising new procedure rules for coercing and repressing the Irish members, and in driving forward their wanton, insidious, and insulting Coercion Bill for Ireland. (Cheers.) It was, therefore, too bad for the prime Minister to say that a gigantic engine of obstruction was being wielded by Mr. Glad- stone, when the "miserable minority" to which he be- longed only numbered one-fourth of the House. He ad- mitted that the progress of the Coercion Bill had been slow, but this was because it had been badly formed, wanting in basis of facts, extravagant and indecent in its objects, and badly mana.gticl from every point of view. (Cheers.) The first clause' of the bill had been expanded through amendments from 34 to nearly, 120 lines. The Government did not know how to draft or conduct their own bill. The complaints of Lord Salis- bury were unmaiily and effeminate. He complained, really, that the Irish, whom we had been flogging for centuries, declined any longer to take their flogging quietly. It was no wonder Lord Salisbury's arm was bred, ,and it would get more and more tired, for it. was impossible permanently to govern a free people by coercion in the light of day and in the atmosphere of freedom which happily pervaded this country. (Cheers.) Everything had been sacrificed to this miser- able bill, which would leave us much farther from the final and necessary solution of the question. If the late Government had been allowed to procPed with its design, the Irish question might have been settled by this time. (Cheers.) The opposition of the Liberal Party to the present Government bill was not because it was an attempt to give more stringency to the law against crime, but becanse It was striking against systems in existence in this country under the name of trades unions. He was confident that the proposed legislation was condemned by the bulk of the people of this country. (Cheers.) He urged them to cultivate a union of sentiment, to extend their know- ledge—especially their historical knowledge of the Irish people—to this extent that they were human beings— (cheers)—full of noble qmilities;and whose defects could be traced to the oppression they had suffered for cen- turies. Ireland was no more made to be governed by force than Wales, or England, or Scotland. This govern- ment by force was at the root of nearly all her miseries and nineteen-twentieths of her sins. If they took their stand upon that undeniable proposition the triumph of their cause was certain, and they would be cheered by the assurance that they had the sympathy, approbation, and prayers on their behalf of the British Empire, of the Anglo-Saxon race, and of civilised Christendom in all quarters of the world. (Loud cheers.) After other speeches the people returned to their homes.

for revision after some experience had been gained on both sides of the Channel. The legend on one of the banners borne in the procession, " The Union of Hearts, not of Manacles," met wit's his warmest approval. In conclusion, be said that he would support a good measure of Home Role without reference to the quarter from which it emana- ted ; and he was hopeful, after his experience of the Cu- duct of the Tories in reference to Catholic Emancipation arid the lowering of the Franchise, that their minds might yet b 3 favourably inclined on this great question. He urged the Liberal party to go forward resolutely to the realisation of the sacred object they had in view. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone subsequently proposed the health 61 Sir Hussey Vivian, which was drunk with musical honours. Three cheers having been given for Lady Vivianand Mrs. Gladstone, the company separated. . RECEPTION OF IRISH EXCURSIONISTS.

Mr. Gladstone attended divine service at Sketty Church on Sunday morning, and on his return was waited upon by a body of excursionists from Cork, numbering 300. The ex-Premier declined to accept any address or to make any speech, but entered into conversation with the High Sheriff and Alderman Madden. Through them he thanked the excursionists for having come such a long distance. '

div.head: COERCION BILL.
div.p: THE COERCION BILL.

_ Mr. SMITH gave notice that on Friday he would move an ;Instruction to the Committee on the Criminal Law Amend- iment (Ireland) Bill the effect of which will be to name a period at which the Committee will report to the House. The House then resumed the consideration of the bill in Committee. Six boars elapsed ere so much as a single ver- bal amendment ceuld be got into the fourth clause. So Mr. Smith imposed The closure at midnight, by which period the first sub-section of tbe clause had been completed. first sub-section of the clause had been completed. With the aid of the closure the first part of the clause was passed through Committee by ten minutes to one, at which time Mr. Balfour, amid the derisive cheers of the Parnellites, moved tbe omission of the second sub-section, thereby abandoning the proposal to transfer certain trials to the Old Bailey. He announced, amid great laughter and a cry of "Coercion Bill No. 2," that a substituted proposal of a Commission of Judges would be introduced in a separate measure.—Sir W. Listrcourer sarcastically congratulated the Ministry on the methods by which they were saving the time of the House, and pointed out, amid great Parcellite cheering, the necessity the Go- vernment seemed to feel themselves under to keep en with Coercion Bills as long a 3 they could, and to stave off remedial measures. A hilarious scene followed when, on Mr. Smith rising to reply to Sir William's criticisms, he had the closure actually imposed on him by Mr. Healy. The hon. member for North Long- ford interrupted him to claim that the question be sow pat. Mr. Smith, amid the prevailing laughter, seemed to be in- timating by his gestures that be had no objection—The Chairman, motioning te the right bon. g-ntleman to resume his seat, at once, put the closure motion, which was carried without division, to the great delight of the Parnellites.— The clause with the Old Bailey sub-section omitted was added to ths bill; progress was reported, and after some other bus:ness had been transacted' the House ad- journed.
