div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

I hear, writes a London correspondent, that Mr. John Morley will be the political direct& of the Daily News. He will not be editor, or charged with the drudgery of editorial work, but he will direct the policy of the paper, and occasionally write in its columns.

• Lord R. Churchill bef leaving Wolverhampton on Saturday received an address from the members of the Bushbury Conservative Association, and told them in reply that he had never doubted that it was perfectly possible to make the principles and policy of the Tory party acceptable to the great masses of the population.

_ Mr. Michael Davitt, addressing a large Nationalist meeting in Dublin County on Sunday, announced that he had just come from Bodyke, and that there had been a cessation of hostilities for the present. His friends across the Channel, who had been terrified by some words he had used the other day, would not find him a very repentant sinner. The advice he gave in view of the Coercion Bill coming into operation was to barricade their doors against the constabulary and military, if ejected to take possession of their holdings again as quickly as possible, if their houses were demolished the neighbours should unite and rebuild them, and in case they were imprisoned the neighbours should contribute towards the alleviation of prison life. He suggested that Mr. Partinll should appeal to the whole'Celtic race at home all abroad for funds to carry out the plan of campaign, and predicted that within six months a mil- lion of money would be raised.

Earl Granville, in addressing the inaagural meeting, on Monday, of the Kent County Liberal Council, over which he presided, at the new National Liberal Club, referred at length to the Irish policy of Her Majesty's Government. He blamed the Ministry for not having accepted Mr. Parnell's bill last year, which, with amend- ments, he thought would have prevented many of the painful evictions now going on in Ireland. It might he wrong to conciliate Ireland, and it might be right ta coerce; but it was certain that one of those two alterna- tives would have to be decided upon. The Land Bill introduced by the Government had been universally condemned, and one of the most staunch and earnest Conservatives bad tobj a Cabinet Minister in his (Lord Granville's) presence that when it reached the House of Commons it would be ignominiously kicked out. The Opposition had been taunted with having formed an alliance with the Parnellites, but while there was a good deal in the past history and in the present actions of the Irish members of which he did not approve, yet that was no reason why they should decline the support of men who constitutionally represented Ireland and whose wish was to solve the problem in the manner most advan- tageous both to Ireland and the Empire.

div.head: DINNER AT SINGLETON ABBEY.
div.p: DINNER AT SINGLETON ABBEY.

In the evening Sir Hussey Vivian entertained a party of about eighty guests th dinner. Sir Hussey Vivian presided, and there were present, besides Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, the Rev. Stephen Gladstohe, and Lady Vivian, Lord Aberdare Lord Kensington, Mr. Aubrey Vivian, several member; of Parliament, and about sixty gentlemen representing the various Liberal associations of South Wales and Monmouthshire. .

----- The CHAIRMAN having proposed the loyal toasts, which were duly honoured, next gave that of Mr. Gladstone, the guest of the evening,. This was received with pro- longed cheering, the whole company rising. Mr. Gladstone proceeded to deal more particularly with the principles on which the two great bills of last year were founded. He denitd that he had regarded Home Rule as a party measure, and deplored the" great loss" which the Liberal party had sustained through the course taken by Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain. Lord Hartington, of whom he should speak but with respect, was what may be called a very moderate Liberal, but the course that be had taken had tended more than anything that had happened for a long series of years to the extinction of what was specially called moderat , Liberalism. Mr. Chamberlain, on the other hand, had been acting, in his opinion, much more in conformity with the generous creed. He knew not whether the desire to advance Radicalism was a leading motive with him in opposing the measure, but he was quite confident that the Opposition tended to drive the Liberal party into a position "which will accentuate all its more profound opinions, and which will throw the weaker and less pronounced opinions that have heretofore found acoeptance within its limits into darkness pr into the shade." The right hon. gentleman re- ferred at considerable length to the question of the exclusion of Irish representatives from the Boos of Commons at Westminster, prefacing this part of his subject with the statement that he would accept Sir G. Trevelyan's sugges- tion of a conference with Lerd Hartington if there was a possibility of good arising out ef it. The question of the retention or the exclusion of the Irish members was one of great importance and difficulty, but it was a I British much more than an Irish question, and he greatly doubted whether this was the proper time for coming to a final resolution on the I subject. He tbrew out a hint that some provisions might be made in the Home Rule Act for bringing up the subject

div.head: SPEECH ON FREE LIBRARIES AND EDUCATION.
div.p: SPEECH ON FREE LIBRARIES AND EDUCATION.

Mr. Gladstone drove into Swansea on Monday, to receive the freedom of the borough and open the Free Library. Shortly before noon a procession, headed by the Police Band, consisting of the Corporation, various local autho- rities, trades and benefit societies, marched through the principal streets from the Town Hall to the Free Library to receive Mr. Gladstone, who arrived at the Library building at 12 30. Crowds lined the thoroughfares, and an immense crowd assembled on the rising ground opposite the Library building, cheering enthusiastically. The streets were profusely decorated, and several build- ings were illuminated at night. In connection with the opening of the Free Library, Mr. Gladstone received two volumes, one containing an illustrated address; the other a catalogue of the books. There was also a golden key, and the freedom of the borough was contained in a handsome casket.

Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Lord Aberdare, and Sir Hussey Vivian, proceeded to the prin- cipal rooms, which had been crowded with is select audience for an lour previously. Here the freedom of the borough was presented by the Mayor of Swansea. The Chairman of the Library Committee read the ad- dress and presented a golden key. Mr. GLADSTONE then declared the building open, and delivered an address. He said that they he. called his attention fro.zi the stormy contention of politics to the field of his predilection, that of literature. Ile then referred to the history of the Free Library movement, to its influence on primary education, which had engendered a desire for the extension of primary education, and the application of means to technical education for labouring classes, especially in those hranches of industry where industry and art joined hands. The success of these educational movements as shown in the marked diminution of crime. lie hoped the action of the State would never reach a point which should lead them not to undervalue volun- tary exertions, or otherwise than to delight in the essociation of public and private effort. An importsat branch of national culture was music, in which Wales excelled, and England must be content to have the second place. He pointed out the enormous progress made in musical education, remarking that a man born entirely without musical faculty was like a man Porn blind, or deaf and dumb. • Let them not suppose these things exhausted their work. As long as man existed there would remain things to be accomplished. Asto the freedom of the borough he was thoroughly convinced that without municipal institutions England would have been a fundamentally different England, and very inferior to the England it was now. lie hoped it would continue not only to enjoy local privileges, but see them extended. He looked forward to the day when millions would, through enact- ments of a solid system of local government. embracing mat, nen-civil, and non-municipal districts, have placed in their reach The benefits from which now they were in &considerable degree excluded; and likewise have the inestimable profit desired by municipal towns, regular education in public duty, reaching downwards to the ranks, and giving English character much of its pro- minence and tenacity of purpose. ENGLAND AND THE IRISH QUESTION.

Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mr-s. Gladstone, the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, Sir Hussey Vivian, Lord Aber- dare' and Mr. Stuart Bendall, left Swansea on Tuesday at 8 40 am en route for London. A number of .persons assembled at the station and cheered him on departing. There were enthusiastic demonstrations at heath, Port Talbot, and Bridgend. The Mayor of Aberavon presented an address from the Town Council, and Mrs. Gladstone was the recipient of a number of bouquets. On his arrival at Cardiff, Mr. Gladstone drove along the principal thoroughfares to Park Hall, to receive an address from the Liberal Association. Spectators crowded the streets, cheering as he passed along, and Bags and bunting were liberally displayed. Park Hall, which is capable of seating 5,000 persons, was densely crowded long before the proceedings commenced, about 1,000 ladies occupying the galleries. Mr. Rees Jones presided, and Mr. Gladstone, on entering the hall, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, was loudly cheered. Tlyi Chairman presented an address of welcome to Mr. Gladstone, who, in reply, said he proposed to speak on the isolation of England in respect to the Irish question. He believed that a decided majority of the English people had the same ideas and wishes as those of Wales, but he had painfully to admit that the great majority of the House of Commons were opposed to them. In speaking of England, he spoke of Parliamentary Eng- land, which was clearly at variance with Wales, Scotland, and Ireland on the Irish question. Over the entire civilised world there was one voice of commiseration and sympathy for Ireland, and one voice of judgment and condemnation for England. In support of this assertion, he referred to the British Colonies, the United States, and Eo.lOpean countries—the mass meet- ings of the former and the literature of the latter. The judgment of the whole world, when they could get it, was worth a great. deal. The Metropolitan Press spoke in a contemptuous man- ner of the remote corners of the country and moun- tainous districts, forsooth! but Wales was supported beyond its own limits. He intended to sound clearly in the earn ot Englishmen this fact, that they were oppos- ing themselves, in the course which their Parliament was pursuing, to the profound sentiment of mankind. There might be consolation if we were able to say we could, nevertheless, manage our affairs satisfactorily. Ent we were not managing our own affairs satisfactorily. Parliament was blocked,and the Coercion Bill was likely to constitute the sole and signal triumph of the Jubilee year. The time would come when the English constitu- encies would find they were wrong, and would listen to the voice of reason and justice, and would end the tragic and miserable policy which had constituted the histoly of England's conduct towards Ireland. The Liberal leader then went on by special train to Newport, where there was another big demonstration in his honour, and a second monstre meeting. There Mr. Gladstone challenged the Government to facilitate the passage of the Crimes Bill by givin., the Irish combina- tion the same protection as English combinations enjoyed, and by abandoning the insulting propcsal to make the bill permanent. At Gloucester he claimed that on Saturday he made' great efforts to show that his object was Imperial and national, and not party, and at Swindon he invited his political opponents to follow the example of Wellington and Disraeli, and themselves propose what the country wanted. He promised Liberal support. The arrival at London at six was devoid of incident. Intense heat prevailed, and many people fainted In crushes at stations.

An exciting scene was witnessed on Sunday night, at Witton, near Birmingham, owing to floods. A brook, which runs across the road, became swollen, and a trap containing a young man and two children was partially submerged in trying to cross it. The children would un- doubtedly have been drowned but for the gallantry of a policeman, who plunged in twice and rescued them. The horse and cart were washed down the stream. INCREASED EMIGRATION.—During May the total num- ber of people who left the United Kingdom for places out of Europe was 51,370, as against 43,534 in the corre- sponding month of 1886. Of the former total 40,233 went to the United States, 7,723 to British North America, 2,279 to Australasia, and 1,135 to all other places. For the five months of the year ended May, the total emigration was 169,618, being an increase of 43,327 upon the corresponding period of 1886, 130,901 going to the United States, 19,443 to British North* America, 12,592 to Australasia, and 6,682 to all other places.

THE RECENT COLLIERY EXPLOSION NEAR WIGAN.—An inquiry was held on Monday by the County Coroner into the explosion at Bryn Colliery, near Wigan, whereby three men lost their lives. The evidence made it clear, and the jury so found, that the explosion resulted from blown-out shots" carelessly ignited in the presence of gas by two of the men killed. Mr. Hall, Government Inspector of Mines, said the sooner blasting was abolished the better it would be for all concerned. Ile and other inspectors had strongly urged that in the new Mines Bill power should be taken to compel every person except shot-lighters to be actually out of the seam while blast- ing was gen on, but he regretted that this advice had not been acted upon. The operation of blasting might produce a violent explosion in a mine which could not be blown up in any other way.

TEE MANCHESTER MURDER—The body of James Dodd, who' on Wednesday, murdered Harriet Turner, a woman with whom he lived, was found on Thursday iu the Ancoats Canal, not far from the scene of the murder. From the first it was supposed that be had made straight for the canal to drown himself, and a diver and drags were en- gaged all Wednesday searching for the body. DECIMALS. COlWAGR.—Replvinz to a deputation who sub- mittsd reasons in favour of the introduction of the decimal system of coinage, Mr. Goachen, on Wednesd4y, stated that the change could not be carried without ast ng opinion in favour of it throughout the country, as it would affect even the smallest corr nttrcial transaction, the whole system of taxation,and the duty OR every article. He mull hold out no hope of proposing in the near future such a measure as the deputation desired.

MR. GLADSTONE'S visit to South Wales xcited great expectations, and it is gratify- ing to be able to state that these expectations have been fully realised. Age cannot stale nor custom wither his infinite variety; the people recognise this, they believe in him, and have made his journey a triumphal pro- gress. He has "witched the world" with noble oratory; he has spoken on Welsh Nationality, on Home Rule, and on National Education; he has touched everything, and adorned everything that he has touched. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and others of his ilk have taken advantage of Mr. GLADSTONE'S silence of late to promulgate the statement that he would make no concession on the question of Home Rule—that he meant to have the bill, the whole bill, and nothing but the bill. It is in vain that the answer has been made that the bill was dead, and that all that was de- manded of Liberals was that they should pledge themselves to carry out, in some form or other, the principle of Home Rule for Ireland. The Liberal Unionists would insist upon wrangling about details; and they have dwelt in particular upon the need, from their point of view, of some concession being made on the question of Ireland being repre- sented at Westminster. Mr. GLADSTONE, as was to be• expected of him, shows himself, exceedingly anxious to promote the union of the Liberal party. Referring to the sugges- tion, on the part of Sir GEORGE TREVELTAN, that there should be a conference between Lord HARTINGTow and himself, he says:—

I say-with regard to that that I accept:the sug- gestion truly and cordially. Ido not think lam in a position to make a proposal to Lord Hartington ; for this reason, that on the last occasion I 'hati a communication with him with regard to Irish j affairs, I found him indisposed to admit that he j ever assented to the constitution of an assembly qualified, under however strict conditions, to act for the whole of Ireland. I know not what is his present state of mind on the subject, but I think I that, after finding him in such a condition as that, it would be impertinence in me to suggest such a , conference. At the same time, if Lord Harting- ' ton should indicate a willingness or desire for such a conference, he will find in me -the readiest response. What could be more open or more candid? If there be no conference, after this pnblic , expression of his readiness, it will be because Lord HARTINGTON does not want to meet Mr. GLADSTONE on this questidn. The in- formation Mr. GLADSTONE has given con- ' firms what we have leng suspected, and that is that Lord HARTINGTON is more Tory than, the Tories themselves in his opposition to Home Rule. We know how Lord CARNAR- YON, as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, held interviews with Mr. PARNELL with the sanc- tion of Lord SALISBURY; but how absurd it seems ta) imagine similar interviews between Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. PARNELL, when there is every reason to doubt whether he will even meet Mr. GLADSTONE to confer on the ! question. The fact is, the heir to the Devonshire Dukedom is a Whirr who has, for the present, gone as tar as he can on the path of progress. The pace is too much for him, and he is content, like the RIP VAN WINKLE that he is, to go to sleeo for a long spell. He does not, like Mr. CITAMBERLMN. say that he is in favour of the principle of Home Rule; he is not in favour of any assembly, however restricted, that shall have power to act for the whole of Ireland. It is curious that tke member for West Birming- ham, who has acted as if he thought Mr. GLADSTONE " stow " chould now find that there is nothing for it but to allow himself to be dragged at the wheels of Lord HARTING• TON'S chariot. It is the penalty, it may be, for his political sins. With regard to the issue that has been raised, as to whether it was still a vital por- tion of the Home Rule scheme that the Irish members should be excluded from West- minster, Mr. GLADSTONE is at much pains to show that it was never treated as an essential feature of the Bill. He has always been entirely free, and is still free, to treat this question—to use his own cxpreSSion—" as policy and good sense may dictate.' AS Lord

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 11, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 11, 1887.

SPENCER has pointed out, it is a matter beset with difficulties, however it is approached ; and, as it is not of first importance, Mr. GLADSTONE is prepared to leave the repre- sentation of Ireland in the English Parlia- ment untouched until some experience of Home Rule has revealed the course which it is most expedient to take. It will be idle, therefore, for the future to contend that the leader of the Liberal party is not prepared to make concessions in order to meet the views of Dissentient Liberals. He has given up all thought of land purchase in Ireland on the lines originally laid down in his Irish Land Bill; and is so far from showing himself un- yielding in another respect, that he regards the question of the retention or exclusion of the Irish members as one " to be dealt with as freely as expediency and the conviction of the country may determine." We must confess that we are not a little puzzled at the anxiety which the Liberal Unionists usually display for retaining the Irish members at Westminster. The followers of Mr. PARNELL are for the most part, if 'the Unionists are to be believed, so rrianv vile conspirators who ; would be hanged if they had their deserts. In the British House of Commons they are arch-pbstructors and mischief-niakers ; and , yet, when there is a chance of getting rid of .
"TOUCH AND GO."
LOCAL NEWS.
It is a pity that Mr. Bright has taken to making unkindly, not to say unwise, refer- ences to his late chief. He cannot injure Mr. Gladstone's reputation, but he can dam- age his own.

It is stated that none of the Irish members will be present at the Jubilee festival in West- minster Abbey. An M.P. who has before him a prospect of being muzzled or im- prisoned by a Coercion Act cannot be ex- pected to feel jubilant.

It is not yet settled whether the Queen will wear the Crown at the Jubilee celebration or —a bonnet. We bet on the bonnet—it is the sovereign emblem of authority amongst the ladies. Besides, the Queen can wear a bon- net on her crown, but she cannot wear her crown on her bonnet.

The Pope is to be specially represented at the Queen's Jubilee; and Her Majesty has expressed her willingness to accept a gift, from the Brothers of the Little Oratory, Brompton, of the works of Cardinal Newman. This is as it should be. The green should be on good terms with all her subjects Orangemen please note, and don't get mad about it.
hem, the Unionists turn rcund-and denounce

those who offer them this ielief. There is no pleasing them; when the Irish members are at St. Stephens they are indignant ; when it is proposed to remove them to College Green they are furious. Lilt Mr. GLADSTONE, with the large heartedness which characterises him, is ready for either course. Perhaps in I urging that the question should be deferred, he f9r.Set,' the time when the matter will be settled by ihe cotistlieen Gf four National Parliaments and one Imperial Parliament. ] For ourselves, the more we consider the Home Rule problem the more we are forced to the conclusion that :this is the only satis- factory solution. We agree with Lord DERBY in saying that it is absurd, by granting Home Rule and retaining the Irish members at Westminster, to say that they shall make , laws for us, but we shall not make laws for I them. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN would urge that it is equally absurd to regard them as part of the United Kingdom and yet not give them a voice in the Imperial Parliament. There are difficulties, we grant, in connection with any narrow application of the Home Rule principle; but extend it as it ought to be ex- tended—follow the principle to its logical issue—and the difficulties vanish. Four Home' Rule Parliaments, one for Ireland, another for Scotland, a third for Wales, and a fourth for England,with an Imperial Parliament corn- p osed of representatives from each local Par- I fament,or of specially-elected members—that is the only scheme which commends itself as theoretically and practically perfect. There are people who say this is Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN'S idea; but if this be so, why does he not advocate it ? Let him cut himself adrift from the Tories and from Lord HA.RTING- TON, and take to preaching Home Rule all

The Jubilee celebration at Coventry is to 'include, it is rumoured, a Lady Godiva pro cession ; but the lady, instead of being clad in silk fleshings, as formerly, is, with her husband, Leofric Earl of Mercia, to b,t at- tired in costumes of the period. This is very much better for everybody, except Peeping Tom, who will think there is nothing to peep at.

According to the latest reports, the Government have decided to abandon the proposal in the Coercion Bill fot changing the venue in certain cases to England, and contemplate substituting a clause providing for trial in Ireland hv a Commission of Judges. This is good as far as it goes, but it would be better still if this abandoned Government would abandon the Coercion Bill altogether.

"Black and White " is the title of a new penny publication which is beina issued in Manchester. The sketches are for the most part cleverly executed; and the portraits are a striking feature. As. in addition, the text is racy and sparkles with fun, the new venture is sure to he patronised by thosa who cal appreciate a good thine..

Another phase of the Sip Canal scheme; a bill is being brought in the House of Com- mons to enable the Company to issue prefer- ence stock. Mr. Whitley, representing Liver- pool of course, objects, and the second read- ing is postponed for a rvek. The bill has been read a first time.

Shinty players will please take warning. Though there is nothing in the Warrington bye-laws in reference to the game, they can be brought up for disorderly conduct. They cannot play shinty in the streets without creating a shindy; a shindy is disorderly, and disorderly conduct is punishable with fine or imprisonment.
round, and we venture to say he will have I half the nation as a following. More than this, he will have Mr. GLADSTONE to help him ; and then the car of progress will be I _ _ _
lifted out of the rut in which' it has stuck, and will go forrard as it ought to do—smoothly, pleasantly, and rapidly.

Mr. Bromley-Davenport, M.P., speaking at the Haydock demonstration on Saturday, said every class was waiting for legislation because Mr. Gladstone would not acceoi his defeat. But he went on to say that Mr. Gladstone had been beaten all to pieces. It is odd, isn't it, that the Tories should be mastered by an opponent who is all in pieces? They must be a poor lot, if they carnot make use of a victory when they have wcai it.

WARRINGTON is singularly unfortunate this year in losing so many of its most prominent sons. We have had to record the death of Mr. WARRINGTON WOOD, of Mr. CHARLES BROADBENT, and Mr. PETER RYLAN DS, and this week the town has been saddened by the sudden death of its most munificent benefac- tor, Mr. GEORGE CROSFIELD. Death, come when and how it will, is in the nature of a shock, and this is especially the case when ' life is shortened by such an accident as that I which befel Mr. CROSFIELD on Monday night. He had been for some time ill, and it was feared that the end might be nigh; but it was I not, of course, anticipated that would be ac- celerated by burning,and byconsequent shock to the system. Mr. CROSFIELD was a man of great capacity, and he was as generous as he was capable. He had peen well trained commercially, and he made such good use of his training, in conjunction with his brother Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD, as to develop a large business at Bank Quay, and acquire a fortune. 'Finding himself in a position to enjoy the luxuries which wealth can procure, he built the beautiful house at Walton Lea, and it speaks volumes for his kindly regard for others 'less favoured by fortune than himself that his first thought was to con- vert the house and grounds into a park for the benefit of the inhabitants of his native town. Further reflection convinced him that Walton Lea was too far beyond the boundary of the borough to be available for such a, purpose; but he was not content to let a generous im- pulse perish still-born. When it was pro- posed to purchase from Lord WINMARLEIGH the house and 'land which now constitute Bank Park, it was proceeded with so far as the Corporation were concerned with the knowledge that MT. CROSVIELD would make the way easy by a munificient gift; but it was not expected that it would result, as it did result, in his contributing £9.500 in order to ensure that Warrington shoul,o have a park large enough for the needs of the day, and for a generation yet nnborn. It need hardly be said that the man who was cap- able of such generosity was actively be- nevolent in other ways. He was a great believer in in the elevating influence of education, and was ever ready with a sub- scription in promoting educational institu- tions. He was throughout life an ardent Liberal,; and was so convinced of the wisdom I of Free Trade years before the principles had becn demonstrated, that he joined his brother. Mr. JOHN CROSEIELD, i„n a ,contribution of £soo to the Cobdelt Testi- monial Fund. The Liberals of Warrington have lost much, but they hardly as yet know how much they have lost, by the untimely death of Mr. GEORGE CROSFIELD. His counsel and his purse were always at their service. Convince him that the object in view was a good one, and unstinted support was a matter of course. Mr. CROSEIELD had for some years resided in London, where he could the better, attend to his duties as irectar .of the London and North-Western Railway and of the North London Railway; but he never ceased to take a deep interest in the affairs of his native town. In was his aim in life to leave the world better than he found it; and he laboured to that end incessantly, unslfishly, and with a nobility of character which is a bright example to his kind.

Mr. Davenport went on to speak of the Liberal Opposition as "a mongrel, half- Radical, half Irish party, under a cantanker- ous leader." This is the language, we sup- pose, of "English gentlemen ;" and if we are to emulate it, we must describe the other side as a gang of plunderers and blunderers, led by a land-grabbing aristocrat whose name is a synornym for a lie.

A St. Helens carter named Dagnall has been sent to gaol for 14 days, for helping himself to coal tt Messrs. Pilkington Bros.' works, where he was employed to remove refuse It was urged for the defence that it was difficult to conceive what benefit it would be to take the coals. But "black diamonds" have some value at St. Helens Surely; and, if they have, it was right to pull the carter over the coals in presence of magistrates by way of teaching him that honesty is the best policy.

"A tug-of-war" was begun at the Haydock demonstration on Saturday; but it was not by any means ended. The Croft lads are in. clincd to think they werevery ill•used in being called upon to pull over their opponents three times, and then be told that there was no decision in their favour. Those who win prizes think they should have them. The tug of war led to a tussle c,f tongues; there was as much bad . language used as if there had been another Tory meeting.

We have not room this week for the usual letter from our London correspondent ; but we take the following tit•bit• as too good to let pass. He says I heard a very good story which requires an apology for thr: telling of it. I hasten to make the apology, and then to tell the tale. I don't say it is true. An Irish member, coming- out of the House in a hurry, ran into the arms of a most malignant Tory. "You're a confounded fool," said the Irish member. " You're drunk," said the malignant fory. "I know I'm drunk," said the Irish member (and indeed he was), "and to-morrow I'll be sober; but to-morrow. you'll be a confounded fool still."

Superintend, nt Barker handed no the certificate of Professor Campbell Brown, who stated that the pepper coutained 20 to 25 per cent of ground olive- stones, a worthless substance imported for the express pur- pose of being used to fraudulently mix with pepper.—The defendant said he purchased the p.pper from tieorge 'Wall, wholesale grocer, Liverpool, and paid Is 21 per lb. for it. The names of the Archdeacons of Liverpool and War- rington are prominently mentioned in connection with the vacant bishopric of Sodor and Man, and the claims of Archdeacon Lefroy are, it is stated, being strongly urged by his political friends. MEASLES EPIDEMIC IN CIIESIIIEE.—An epidemic of a most disastrous character is raging at Wins- ford. The whole of the schools in the town are closed. One medical man has treated over 200 patients, and 21 deaths have been recorded down to the present moment. As many as six children have been down with the disease in the same family. WELL SINKING EXPLOIT.—" The Macclesfield Courier" says :—An extraordinary feat has just been performed at the North Cheshire Brewery. This brewery has a bore hole in the earth 225 ft. deep, and about 20 years ago a large boring tool was lost at the bottom. It could not be recovered, and has lain there ever since. Messrs Kilner• and Matthews have been repairing the bore hole, and, finding the boring tool in their way, at once deter- mined to have it out. Accordingly, on Saturday last, they commenced to get it up, and at 3 o'clock on Monday they brought it to the surface. It is a very curious relic, and when it is considered how long it has been at the bottom of the hole, and the efforts that were made to get it up when it was lost, we think great credit is due to the skill and enter- prise which has been displayed by Messrs Kilner and Matthews in performing so difficult a task. We may say.that it is in a capital state of preserva- tion,

large room at Arpley Station. ith regard to politics, it is well known that Mr. George Crosfield, like his brother, Mr. John Gros- field, has always been an ardent. supporter of the doctrines of advanced Liberalism, and in earlier (lays he formed one of that noble band of reformers who, under the leadership of Mr. Cobden, spared neither person nor purse in the struggle for politi- cal and social progress. Towards the testimonial [which was presented to Mr. Cobden, Mr. George Crosfield, along With his brother, Mr. John Crosfield, contributed £6OO as a token of his appreciation of the services rendered to the State by the great reformer. While living in Warrington Mr. Cros- field was always to the front in connection with local political movements. In 1868, when Mr. Peter Rylands was returned at the head of the poll in his contest with Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. George Cros- field was the chairman of the Liberal party in War- rington, and when the Conservatives petitioned against the return he contributed Very largely to the fund raised for the defence of the sitting mem- ber's rights. That petition was heard before Mr. Baron Martin, who in the end declared Mr. Rylands to be duly elected. During that, election of 1868 Mr. Crosfield also had the honour of entertaining Mr. Gladstone, who was contesting South-West Lancashire. Since that time Mr. Crosfield has often presided over the gatherings of local Liberals, and even since his removal to London he has often given proof that his interest in the fortunes of the party locally had in no wise abated. Mr. Crosfield was made a county magistrate in , 1869, but declined to permit himself to be nominated ' to the local bench. In addition to being a director on several smaller concerns, including the North London Railway. Mr. Crostield was one of the directors of the London and North-Western Railway, and in this capacity he has earned golden opinions by his business abilities and by the solicitude he has always shown for the welfare of the innumerable employes of this great company. It should be mentioned that in religion Mr. Crosfield was a mem- ber of the Society of Friends. He leaves a wife and one daughter, the latter having married Mr. C. N. 'Nicholson, barrister.__

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

Our London correspondent has furnished the fol- lowing full report of the proceedings at the inquest held by Dr. Danford Thomas, coroner for one of the divisions of Middlesex, on the body of Mr. Crosfield. The inquest was held in a Mission Hall off the Edgeware-road, one of the main tho- roughfares of London, and was timed for eleven o'clock. At a few minutes to eleven the metropoli- tan police in attendance summoned the jury to view the body. On their return, accompanied by the coroner, they were formally empannelled, and the coroner read the depositions which had been fur- , nished to him, remarking that the details would• be corroborated in the evidence about to be given, but that the chief allegations appeared to be that Mr. Crosfield, having retired to rest at his usual early hour of nine o'clock, accompanied by Mrs. Crosfield, had had a table placed at his bedside bearing light articles of invalid diet, a candle, and matches. About eleven o'clock Mrs. Crosfield was aroused, and finding the room on fire, conveyed her husband into his dressing room ad- joining, whence, for some reason unknown, but supposed to be the obtaining of his watch and keys, in her temporary absence to obtain help he returned to the burning room, his night clothes caught fire, and he fell upon the bed over- come by the smoke. The first witness called stated, in answer to the coroner: My name is Joseph John Crosfiedd, and the deceased was my uncle, a gentleman of independent means residing at 109, Lancaster Gate, Hyde Park. I do not live with him, but am occasionally in Lon- don for a few days at a time, and then always stay at his house. On Monday evening I left him at dinner about seven o'clock to go to a theatre. He was a great invalid, suffering from lumbago and rheumatism, and unable to walk without support, but during dinner he more than once remarked how well he felt, and that he had enjoyed greater free- dom from pain that day than had been the case for many months. That was the last time I saw him conscious and well About eleven I returned to the house, and had only been in a few minutes when I heard my aunt screaming for help. I rushed up to the bedroom that my uncle and aunt occupied con- jointly, found dense volumes of smoke coming through the curtains, and saw my uncle sitting on the side of the bed in the midst of the fire. I entered the room and endeavoured to extinguish the fire and drag him out, hut was driven back by the smoke, and he was too much burnt for me to hold him. With the assistance, however, of the cook and the footman, William, he was dragged to the doorway and out of the smoke. Finding that he was unconscious and apparently dying, the doctor was sent for and promptly arrived, but could give us no hope of a recovery. 3,fy uncle lingered until a little past two, insensible for the greater part of the time, and then died. He was very weak and feeble, having always to be assisted up and down stairs. The next witness called deposed :" My name is William Charles Robinson, and I was under footman to the late Mr. Crosfield. It was part of my duty to assist him up and down stairs, and on Monday evening I helped him to his room about half-past eight, and left him there to be undressed by his own servant. He had a small table by his bedside with beef tea, soup, candle, and matches upon it, as he frequently wanted food during the night. He generally lit a good many matches. I did not particniarly notice the table and candle on Monday evening, and did not place It there, but I know it was his habit to have it, and it must have been there. About eleven o'clock 1 heard the bedroom bell rung violently, and on going upstairs found Mr. Crosfield sitting on the burning bed. Mr. John Crosfield was there and the cook. Together we dragged him out of the room on to the landing. He was quite insensible, and I do not think he spoke again. Dr. Gifford Randsford, M.D., deposed: I was Mr. Crosffeld's constant medical attendant, and he hap been under my care especially since September last suffering from rheumatism and lumbago. His limbs were affected, rendering him unable to walk with- out assistance, and very shaky in his hands. He was in such a generally weak state that I consi- dered it necessary for him to have food always at hand, even in the night, and for this reason directed beef. tea, soup, or any other light refreshment that he , fancied to be placedat his side. This was always done.' About eleven o'clock on Monday night I was sent for, and on reaching the house found my patient suffering from severe burns, and in a state of tol- lapse. There was from the first no hope of recov- ery, and he died about half-past two. He was par- tially conscious, but did not speak. Mrs Crosfield, who was in the room with him at the time, is now j under my care suffering from nervous shock, and I unable to leave her bed but she has been able to i tell me all she knows about the painful occurrence. It seems that about eleven o'clock she was awoke by a sensation of great heat, saw Mr. Crosfield sit- ; ting at the root of the bed, and the curtains at the side blazing. She opened the dressing room door with difficulty, and having assisted her husband into the room and on to a sofa, went out on to the stairs to summon help. On turning back she found that Mr. Crosfield had disappeared into the smoke of the bedroom, and when rescued a minute or two later he was found in a prone position on the bed in ' the midst of the spreading flames. I Can only con- jecture myself that Mr. Crosfield in endeavouring to light his candle dropped the lighted match on the valance of the bed, thereby setting fire to it. He may have returned to the burning room for his

The ordinary monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council, was fixed to be held in the Council Chamber at the Town • Hall, on Tuesday evening, but no business was transacted, the meeting being adjourned as aimark of respect to the deceased, after a vote of condolence with the bereaved relit. tives had been passed. The Mayor,(Alderman Pick- mere) presided, and there were also present Alder- men J Burgess, S Chrindley, J Davies, J Harrison, C J Holmes, T H Sutton; Councillors J. Ashton, Barker, W Bolton, J Brown, F Dixon, E Greenall, jun., J Greening, J Hutchinson, T Jollm T Litton, W Marsh, J Pierpoint, W Pierpoint,FJ Platt, F A Roberts, H Roberts, W Tinsley; W H Brook (town clerk), J L Whittle (deputy town clerk). C Chorley (borough treasurer), T Longdin (borough surveyor), and J Paterson (gas manager. On taking his seat the MAyon said: I have no doubt you have all heard, as I have, with extreme regret, of the lamentable death of Mr. George Cros- field. I have no doubt that some of you were, as I was myelf, personally intimate with him, and it has grieved me exceedingly to hear what has happened. The shock has come upon us so suddenly that I can scarcely say *what I feel on the subject, but I am sure you will all agree with me in passing a resolu- tion condoling with the family of the deceased in their great loss. (Hear, hear.) I will move the resolution, and suggest to the Council that we ad- journ from this evening to this day week out of respect to the deceased and his family. • The resolu- tion I have to move is--" That this Council receive with deep regret the announcement of the death of George Croslaeld. EN., which took place te‘day, and beg to express their heartfelt sympathy and condo- lence with Mrs. Crosileld and her family on the sad event."

Alderman Buttons, in seconding the motion, said: I assure you that it is with feelings of the greatest yain and sorrow that I rise to second the proposition now made. I have known Mr. Crosfield the whole of my life in Warrington, which is for more than 50 years. I knew him in connection with this Corpbration. Forty years ago this month of June he entered ' the Corporation as one of its members. Thirteen years ago this month of June this Corporation took possession of the Town Hall, largely through the liberality and generosity of Mr. Crosfleld. who had the best interests of Warrington at heart as much, and more, than most men I have known; and his lamented end is one which fills us with great anguish and regret. (Hear, hear.) I hope there will be a resolution of condolence forwarded to the widow and family, and I hope we shall long be spared before we witness another event so start- ling in its character, so sudden, as the death of Mr. Crosfield. (Hear, hear.) Alderman DAVIES : Before we separate I desire to say a few words Perhaps it there is any mem- ber of this Council who feels more than another the powerful influence that was ukd in promoting the interests of Warrington perhaps lam that man. I can hardly tell the Council of the many occasions this Corporation has received the able support of Mr. Crosfleld, not only in money, but with influence and ehcouragement to us to progress in what we were doing for the benefit of our town. As Alder- man Burgess has just said, Mr. George Crosfield was highly instrumental in our getting this beauti- ful building for our Town Hall. I confess to you that at one time I almost broke down in carrying out the negotiations for the purchase, and had it not been for the powerful influence and support which was given to me by the late Mr. Crosfield, Alderman Holmes, ,and the then Councillor Sutton, at one stage of the negotiations I think they might .pos- sibly have fallen through. That is only one Inci- dent in the life of Mr. Crosfield to show that he was . .

I bound up in his native town of Warrington; and, although he left us many years ago, he has always taken a warm and deep interest in the welfare of the town. (Hear. hear.) His is a sad and lament- able end. Mr. Crosfleld seemed to have attained, and deservedly attained, every desirable thing in this life, but it seems that Providence has shown him what h. thousand ways there are out of this world. Notwithstanding everything that could be done to conduce to Mr. Crosfield's comfort during a long and serious illness, lie has met with the de- pl. rable end of which we have heard, and which is overcoming even to us who are so far away from him. I can hardly express all I would say. I never felt so keenly the death of anyone outside my own family. . - -

Councillor F. A. ROBERTS: As the youngest mem- ber of the Council, and certainly as the last to be initiated into this Chamber, I desire to add my testimony to what has already fallen from the lips of the Mayor and of Aldermen Burgess and Davies, with regard to the sincere regret we all feel in hear- ing of our sad bereavement. I think we might, in addition to the suggestion of the Mayor of adjourn- ing the Comicil for a week, arrange for a deputation to attend on behalf of the Council at the funeral of Mr. Geo. Croslield. If I ant out of order in making such a suggestion, perhaps the Mayor will take it as a supplementary resolution. Ido think, as a new corner politically into Warrington, that we owe a great deal to Mr. George Crosllekt: Those who have been practically allied to him—though this is not a political chamber—have the highest and the heartiest sympathy with his family in this very sad bereavement; his death is indeed a great loss to us, and we feel it to be so to the utmost degree. (Hear, hear.) - The resolution was the* put to the meeting and carried unanimously. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor DIXON secon- ded, the adjournment of the Council till the 14th inst., which was agreed to. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS asked what was the decision of the Council with reference to the de- putation from the Council attending the funeral, and Alderman BURGESS remarked that he did not think it necessary to appoint a deputation. If the funeral took place in the district, as it in all pro- bability would, no doubt all the members of the Council would attend. (Hear, hear.) The Council then rose. MEETING AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

On Wednesday evening a largely attended meeting of the Liberal General Council was held at the Liberal Club at which a vote of condolence with Mr. George Crosfield's family was passed. Mr. J. G. McNlinoiee presided, and amongst others preemie were Alderman Burgess, Dr.Gornall, Councillor F. A. Roberts, Councillor W. Pierpoint, Coon- ! aloe T. Greening, Mr. J.Ninsar, Mr. C. S. Burgess, Mr. J. 'Walker, Mr. R. Roberts, dsc.

THE Cnainarmv said be supposed he should have some difficulty in persuading his friends that be acted prudently In being there that night, genial and charming as the even- ing was, but on that occasion be found it quite impossible to absent himself from that meeting considering the object they had in view. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Crosfield was one of the oldest, one of the most intimate, one of the truest, and 000 of the roost esteemed friends he had in the world. (Hear, hear.) He had known Mr. Crosfield intimately for fifty years, and they had been associated together in many works, political and other, for that term of years. He thought that when he first knew Mr. Crosfiell in connection with politics it was about the year 1841. The Liberal party bad suffered a great and unexpected defeat in 1837, after mak- ing very great exertions to win. After this defeat in 1837, the Liberal party languished for many years, and at the general election in 1841, when under the influence of the Anti-Corn Law League they proposed to fight the borough they found that everything had been so neglected—the ; registration and every other kind of organisation connected ; with the party—that they were in a stateef hopeless despon- ' dency. They did not fight a battle in 1841, for their can- didate Mr. Kershaw retired before the poll. It was then determined that the party should be re-organised and under the presidency of Holbrook Gaskell—nut the present Hol- brook Gaskell, but his uncle—the party was re-organised and the town was divided into five districts, very much corresponding to the five wards into which the borough was afterwards divided when it was incorporated. To every one of these divisions a secretary was appointed. They were all youpg men, and Mr. George Crosfield was one of them. (Hear, hear.) Ever since that time Mr. Crosfield had taken an earnest and active part in politics on the side of Liberalism—(hear, bear)—and knowing him as he (the chairman) bad known him he had no hesitation in saving that by his death the Liberal party. in Warrington had suf- fered the greatest loss they could possibly have sustained. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Crosfield had been an earnest, an active, a generous and an open-hearted man throughout all the years he had known him,and he did not know that, especially to the

younger members of the party, he could say anything bett than to ask them to fo low in his footsteps. (Hear, hear.) After 1841, and after the re-organisation of the party they did fight a pitched battle in 1847 and they were defeated. Notwithstanding everything that they believed they could do they suffered a signal defeat. From 1847 to 1868 Greenallism reigned supreme in Warrington, but in 1868 they again attacked the enemy and beat them ; they beat them again in 1880—(hear, hear)—and he supposed they would beat them again some time hereafter. (Applause.) I Now throughout all those years they had Mr. Crosfield at their side, and be was never wanting when anything that he could do would promote the interests and the suc- cess of the Liberal party. They owed to the late Mr. Crosfield a debt of gratitude which it would be quite im- possible for him to describe. (Hear, bear.) They were met together in order to express their feelings in reference to that bereavement and the first thing they had to do would be to move and carry a resolution of condolence with Mrs Crosfield and the late Mr. Crosfield's family. (Ap- plause) Mr. F. A. ROBERTS said that perhaps their chairman had already paid the highest tribute they as an association could pay to their late vice-president, by being present at that meeting, for they all knew that in Mr. McMinnies present state of health it was a great trial and exertion for him to come to a heated meeting. He was sure that when Mrs. Crosfield heard that Mr. McMinnies had been able to preside at that meeting she would feel that that tribute of respect was all the greater from that association. (Hear, hear.) The chairman had told them very fully what Mr. Crosfield had done for the Liberal party, but he took it that they would also express their gratitude for what Mr. Gros- field had done for Warrington, and he thought that all of them who enjoyed their public park and Town Hall knew that they mainly owed these advantages to Mr. George Crosfield's generosity. (Hear, hear.) It was princely gene- rosity to Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McMineies had told them what they as a party owed to Mr. George Cros- field, and he eould only say for himself that coming into the field there almost at a time when Mr. George Croafield had left off work—though he had enjoyed one or two public meetings in the Public Hall, under his presidency—yet he knew that they had never lost him as an active supporter of their party in every way. In his generosity to its funds, Mr. George Crosfield had been the backbone of that association, even up to his death. But be did not think that their feelings of respect would spring altogether from what Mr. Crosfield had done for them in that respect, but rather from regarding him as a man and as a benefactor to his native town of Warrington. He would move a reso- lution which he felt certain would be carried unanimously by that association. It read as fellows :—"That the mem- bers of the Warrington Liberal Association have learnt with feelings of the most profound regret of the unexpected and painful death of their valued friend and vice-president the late Mr. George Crosfield, Erg., and while placing upon record their high appreciation of the invaluable services rendered by him to the cause of Liberalism in Warrington for to many years past, would at the same time respectfully offer to Mrs. Crosfield and the family their sincere and heartfelt sympathy in the sad bereavement which bas so suddenly befallen them." (Hear, hear.) Mr. S. Rae Low said he cordially seconded the proposi- tion. He did think that in all their experience of public affairs in Warrington they never had a gentleman who so thoroughly supported his party, and supported everytbing for the good of the town as Mr. George Crosfield. (Hear, hear.) He believed that Mr. Crosfield was thoroughly un- selfish in whatever he did for the progress of the town. He was a kindly-hearted and sound-hearted man. a man who was an ornament to the town and a man who in political life he (Mr. Barlow) would liked to have seen representing the town in Parliament. He believed that Mr. Crosfield was really and truly a thorough Warringtonian, and that his heart and soul was in the town in which he had lived, and in which his father had lived. They should emulate the deceased gentleman's conduct, for a more unselfish man never was born. (Hear, hear.) He was one of the twin. dens of the school from which he (Mr. Barlow) received his little education' that was the Newton-street British Schools, now transferred to the People's College, and beyond that they knew that his purse had been unlimited in reference to social matters. (Hear, bear.) Even a few days before his death he performed an act of munificence, to the town which was, perhaps, unknown to them, but was known to him (Mr. Barlow). (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. PIERPOINT said he could hardly allow an occa- sion of that kind to go by without saying a few words upon the oubject that had called them together. It brought back to him painful recollections. It seemed only the other day that they were engaged in passing a similar resolution in respect of a very old and valued friend—he was referring to the late Mr. Charles Broadbent. With Mr. Broadbent be had had a long and valued connection, and he thought their acquaintance was mutually agreeable, but with respect to Mr. Crosfield his (Mr. Pierpoint's) connection with Liberal- ism in Warrington was of such a recent date that he must admit he never came very much into contact with Mr. Geo. Cresfield except as treasurer of that association. He must, however, acknowledge that at all times Mr. Crosfield had been ready to assist whenever occasion demanded such as- sistance. (Hear, hear.) As a meml2er of the Warrington Corporation he felt deeply indebted to Mr. Croafield, because it was through his munificence that he was able to perform his duties in that Corporation with a greater degree of com- fort than the Corporation could do prior to his munificent gift. It was an undoubted fact that bad it not been for the munificent conduct of their late friend, they, as a Cor- poration would net have been in posaeesion of the Town Hall they had now, and which would be good enough for the town for the next fifty years. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Bar- low had spoken of Mr. Crostield's connection with the New- ton-street Schools, and he dare say that if they knew all Mr. Crosfield had done with reference to education in War- rington their eyes would be opened very considerably. (Hear, hear.) It was an undoubted fact that the town is in possession of a magnificent school of art, as complete in all its arrangements as most schools of art in towns of similar • size, and he believed that fact was due also to the munifi- cence of the family of Croefield. (Hear, bear.) He could only say with their chairman, that he thought the example of the life of their late friend was one that ought to stir up in them such a spirit of emulation that they would try to maintain as good a name in their party as that he had left behind him. (Hear, hear.) Dr. GoRNALL said he could not resist the temptation to say how grieved he felt at the sad trouble that had come on the family of Crosfield. He wished also to say, as medi- cal officer of health, that the people of Warrington were more indebted to Mr. Croefield's beneficence in providing a park, than to any other benefit that had been bestowed on Warrington. And, politically speak- ing, he felt that if the landlords of Ireland had the heart that the late Mr. Crosfield had, and that their worthy president had, the scenes which disgraced the sister island during the present and the past week would never have occurred. (Hear, hear). Mr. T. FLOOD geld he did not know of an occasion when he felt more grief than be felt on the first announcement of the death of Mr. Crosfield. He was personally considerably indebted to him for the kindness he had received at his bands, and as a railway servant he felt that it would be a long time before Mr. Crosfield's Place could be filled with a man of equal capacity. (Hear, bear). • Mr. Joust HOLDING alluded to the feelings of regret ex- pressed by a large number of ironworkers, Conservatives as well as Liberals, on hearing of the sad event. (Hear, bear).

Mr. T MILLER said he recollected Mr. Crosfield's father, who was a vary energetic man in political matters. The late Mr. Crotifield had always been -faithful to his party, and las (Mr. Miller) believed that the party by his death had sustained one of the greatest misfortunes. (Hear, hear.) Mr. C. S. BURGESS said he had not had any very intimate association with Mr. George Croafield, bat he had known some little about him. As a politician, he thought that everyone in that mom must acknowledge that he was one of the foremost they had ever had in Warrington, and one whom they might well endeavour to imitate. (Hear, hear.) He was a gentleman who did what he could in his day and generation, and there were few in Warrington who had done as meph. If they had enly a few more men as sturdy and honest as Mr. George Croitheld the world would be better worth living in. (Hear, hear.) Mr. STIRRUP said he knew Mr. Crosfield when he was a young man, and before be came out as a politician, but from that time till this he had been a consistent lover of the People. From the time of his youth upi he had been one of nature's noblemen. (Hear, hear.) Than Mr. P. Rylands, Mr. George Crosfleld, and Mr. McMinnies, they had never had three better men in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Mr. G. WALLINGTON said he had met Mr. George Cros- field many times in his life, and always regarded him with pleasure, as be was a representative man, and always had the good of the town at heart. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS said they had lately had several severe bereavements in Warrington, which had fallen with great weight on the Liberal party. Men who had been serving for years, from boyhood up to old age, had been taken away from them within a very recent period. There were Mr. Broadbent and Mr. Peter Rylands, and then Mr. Crosfield bad gone. Their places were not easy to fill, for they were men of marked intelli- gence, very assiduous, very determined, and exceedingly honest in their parsnite. They were Liberals because they felt what the value of Liberalism was to the people of this country, and for himself, he could only say that he could have wished that their lives had not been taken away quite so early. (Hear, hear.) It was for them to take care that the banner was kept afloat, and that it was carried erect and aloft, and they would do more by doing that to sho* their appreciation of the work of those men he had been speaking of than by anything else they could do. What those men bad done, he said unto them, "Go thou and do likewise." (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. ROBERTS said that, haying had te de with Mr. Croafield upon many matters of private and per- sonal character— not for himself, but for other sup- pliants —he could say this, that a more kindly- disposed man, a man whose disposition it was to give generously rather than carefully, be never met in all his life. (Hear, bear.) He could not help being impressed also with the magnificence of his character as a business man. They knew perfectly well what the large concern at Bank Quay was, but few of them had the remotest idea of the capacity, energy, and ability Mr. Croafield brought to bear upon the business relations of the London and North- Western Railway Company. As had been said his place in connection with that concern would not be easily filled. (Hear, hear.) In his private and commercial life he (Mr. Roberts) believed Mr. Crosfield wore the white flower of a blameless character, and no one could breathe one word against Mr. Crosfield in either of those capacities. (Hear, hear).

Total WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.—Tbis match was played at Broughton on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the visitors by twelve runs The visitors came with only a weak team, having S. M. Croafield, Bettisworth, and their new " pro" (Tinsley) absent. Payne won the toss, and, no doubt thinking to give the visitors a chance, put them in. The wicket was very slow, and the scoring off the bowling of Murphy and Kentfield was not extraordinary,the amateur suffering most. Armstrong was taken at slip, Clarke from a long drive, and Ford was clean bowled. The last.named had played well for his runs. Denton was taken smartly at wicket and on Moggeridge joining Crosfield the only stand was made. Moggeridge played freely, and put the ball over the spectators to the long on. At GO Moggeridge was out lbw, a decision he evidently did not like. Wickets fell fast, and nine runs were put on for the last wicket, the sub- stitute being bowled by a good ball from Sawyer. This bowler obtained 5 wickets for 22 runs. Broughton com- menced with J. H. Payne and Heap. Thirteen were scored, when a forward bit was intercepted by Clark, and Heap run out. Payne was almost immediately missed by the same fielder from an easy chance, but at the same score (25) Denton clean bowled his wicket. Nearly an hour had elapsed, and 25 runs only had been put on for two wickets. So well did the bowling keep on that runs were very slowly added. The wicket was now extremely diffi- cult, and helped the bowlers greatly. Lyon stepped in front and Was lbw to Denton, and Kentfield was grandly caught in the long field by Moggeridge. Sawyer was also lbw after a few mid-hits, and Murphy tried in vain to save the game. No batsman conld withstand the bowlers Cros- field got the ball to work finely, and his three last wickets cost nine runs, in addition to two chances being let off. Harrison hit out and gave a chance to stump. but was bat* in time. Murphy was the one hope, and the spectators loudly applauded each run. He was secured at last by Meg- geridge in the slips. It was a splendid catch, quite close to the ground, the fielder falling rather heavily in holding the ball. Denton got Smith in an, almost similar manner two flyers previously. Boyd gave no trouble, and the innings closed for 75. With the exception of three chances, the fielding was smart all round, but Moggeridge undoubtedly took the palm. His fielding in the out field saved many runs, while the catch that dismissed Murphy was declared te be one of the best ever seen: Analyes : Denton, 23 overs, 10 maidens, 23 runs, 5 wickets. WOMAN FROM AUSTRIA. A WOMAN FROM AUSTRIA. A. WOMAN FROM AUSTRIA. NEAR THE VILLAGE OF ZILLINGDORF, in Lower Austria, lies Maria Haas, an intelligent and indus- trious woman, whose story of physical suffering and final relief, as related by herself, is of interest to English women. "I was employed," she says, "in the work of a large farmhouse. Overwork brought on sick headache, followed by a deathly fainting and sickness of the stomach, until I was unable to retain either food or drink. I was compelled to take to my bed for several weeks. Getting a little better from rest and quiet, I sought to do some work, but was soon taken with a pain in my side, which in a little while seemed to spread over my whole body, and throbbed in my every limb. This was followed by a cough and shortness of breath, until finally I could not new, and I took to my bed for a second, and, as I I thought, for the last time. My friends told me that say time had nearly come, and that I could not live longer than when the trees put on their green once more. Then I happened to get one of the Seigel pamphlets. I read it and my dear mother bought me a bottle of Seigel's Syrup, which I took exactly according to directic-ns, and I bad not taken the whole of it before 1 felt a change for the better. My last illness began June the 3rd, 1882, and continued to August 9th, when I began to take the Syrup Very Boon I could do a little light work. The cough left me, and I was no more troubled in breathing. Now lam perfectly cured. And oh, how happy I am! I cannot express enough gratitude for Seigel's Syrup. Now I must tell you that the doctors in our district distributed handbills cautioning people against the medicine, telling them it would do them no good, and many were thereby influenced to des- troy the Seigel pamphlets; but now wherever one is to be found it is kept like a relic. The few pre- served are borrowed to read, and I have lent mine for six miles around our district. People have come eighteen miles to get me to buy the medicine for them, knowing that it cured me, and to be sore to get the right kind. I know a woman who was look- ing like death, and who told them there was no help for her, that she had consulted several doctors, but none could help her. MINING ROYALTIES.—No. 2.
BY H. WIIITHAM.

In large coalfields like those in the North the privi- lege of carrying over the lands of numerous land. . owners must no longer be of a capricious character ; indeed, must no longer be a privilege, but calls for the ! early settlement of the larger question, that is as to ; the true and only possible ownership of the land. Seven years ago, when depression was said to exist in Germany, Prince Bismark constituted a Council of National Economy to inquire into the state of trade I in the different parts of Germany, urging this Conn- ! oil also to advise the Government where any matters j affecting trade had to be dealt with. At the time of appointing this Council the Prince pointed out " the want of really competent advice in matters of trade in times of emergency, and the absolute necessity of some practical organisation to advise and work with the Government on questions of trade and commerce and agriculture." Can anyone doubt that this is what we urgently want here ? Such a council, composed of men taken from the two classes representing labour aad capital, would do much towards advising Govern- ment as to the requirements of the present altered Istate of things, and would do more than anything else towards carrying the nation peacefully through the present transition epoch. Before leaving the coal question a few words may be said respecting the evidence of Mr. Alfred Hew- lett, managing director of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company. This firm, producing nearly 2,000,000 tons I of coal and iron per year, is, one would think, very ;I much interested in the question pf royalties. The evidence put in stated that 100,000 tons of iron is at , present produced, although only "one half of our fur- naces' are at work owing to the depression, and about 10,000 workmen employed. The evidence of this gentleman is extremely in- teresting, as, while he distinctly states that royal- ties in England are" four times as high as in West- phalia," he still says "for the collier, I think the rate of wages ought to be reduced." In Germany and Westphalia it seems that the royalty paid is a per centage of the selling price of fuel at the pit's mouth, and that per centage is two per cent., whereas in Eng- land the royalties are generally fixed at a certain amount per ton, and the average in England is about eight per cent. In this district is is between nine . and ten per cent. In Westphalia the mines belong to the State and the royalty is fixed by the State officials. Will it be believed that this witness strongly urges , that the present system of 'private bargain" should continue ? Although he acknowledges it is one of "the causes of the depression in the coal trade at present." Speaking of "dead rents," he says—" If I take a lease from a landowner he probably will ask .me, say £l,OOO a year, and 61 per ton royalty, or what- ever it may be, and I have to pay that £l,OOO a year whether I get any coal or whether I do not get any coal. If I get ..E3OO worth of coal one year, and I get £1,500 worth the next year, I pay £l,OOO etich year. In other words, the landlord must have his £l,OOO whether you get any coal or not." • As a mat- ter of fact, this firm has paid £260,000 for the right to get coal in the future. Here we see an eighth of the capital of this firm, with all its potential powers, paid ' away to a landowner who gives nothing whatever in re- I turn ; and should the lessee go tothe landowner when his lease is just expiring and say "1 have over-paid £20,000 to you, will you give me 20 years longer, or 10 years longer, to get that coal," he would say "I am a limited or life owner only, and I have no power to do it."

In the Wigan Coal and Iron Comnany's district £l,OOO a week is paid for dead work, of which nothing WAS known, when the pits were sunk. Workmen need ask no longer where their wages go. nor yet, ail for reasons for the con- tinued had state of trade. Confiscation, or no confiscation, a drastic and sweeping measure is the only cure that can be thought of, for in the case of this company the manager states he has " given up all hopes of getting his certain rents reduced," although on coal not worth more than 5s 6d per ton, an average royalty of 6d per ton his paid. Now let us turn to the other, and I think no less impor- tant question of royalties in connection with the iron trade. To those who have given a little of their time to the consi- deration r,f this subject. I need scarcely say that from the year 1800 to the present time the history of the iron trade is the history of the development of British Industries and that the secret of our suoceas is to be found in the practical monopoly we have enjoyed not only in skilled labour and natural facilities, but iu being the chief producers for the whole of the known world. This is now all altered ; other nations have ceased to be our customers and have become producers. Our exhibitioes and workshops have been opened to them, and the German, Belgian. and American workman has been an apt learner. Taking us as their guide they have avoided our mistakes, and, as we have seen in the case of coal royalties, have kept in the hands of the State, what must otherwise have been their utter ruin, that is the right to use nature's bounteous gifts for the natioos welfare, and not for the individuals, the right to use the land for all railway purposes, and its minerals for purely commercial purposes. To show how important it is, that we should at once cast off all the supposed rights of the individual in so far as it is a tax on commerce I may point out that the values of
.--- E s. d. , E s. d. Cleveland pig in 1872 4 17 1 In March, 1888...1 10 9 Eltafferdahlre bars Bteel mite In 1874 &4 5 0

During all these years, with few exceptions, the landlord's royalty rent has been paid, but the workman's wages have decreased. We are in no danger of our trade being ciippled for want of ores; and figures could be given showing what we have done and what we could de if we would only use the power now in our hands. No false respect for the rights of others should prevent us asking why the lord of the manor should receive £lO,OOO a year in the shape of ground rents from property at Openshaw,. near Manchester. Here we have a gentleman who is non-resident, and who does not contribute a penny to the rates. Can anyone say why the city of London should tax London industries, the London poor, and the collier to the extent of £450,000 nett per year ? Surely not. Sir Lowtbian Bell, questioned as to the power of the Germans to produce cheaper, and deliver in this country cer- tain articles, such as girders, steel, said, "I do not think that Germany can from her ores produce steel and deliver it in this country cheaper than we can manufacture it from our own ores, and that the same argument would apply to the sale of girders which at one time was pretty large in this country." Now as a matter of fact we know girders and other arcicles do come bare, rather too freely,and we prefer to look for the cause, when we know we shall find it. and not as the Fair Trader suggests, by cutting our noses off to spite our faces. Were I dealing with tbe railway car- riage question some astonishing figures could be produced, land I only allude to it now to point oat that railway charges ;coal rents, and royalties, added to royalties on ore, combine I to answer all questions respecting our inability to keep the foreigners out of oar markets. More than this, evidence tends to show that if we had not there taxes on the raw ma- terial, we should have been able to tender for the erection of the Brooklyn suspension bridge, instead of which, al- though every wiredrawer in England was invited to tender. not one could comply with the conditions. It is necessary to fully understand the question of royal- ties that their payment may be reckoned in various ways. j In Germany the ownership of coal and iron ore is vested in ;the State. The royalty paid on the former is 2 per cent, on the profits. At a selling price of Bs per ton the profits will 'be such that lid per ton will cover this payment. For iron ore nothing is paid for the right of working. This pay- ment fore right of working" is in England nailed fixed rent, of which I will give examples further on. Royalty I charges are as follows In Great Britain: Pig iron per ton, Cleveland, 3s ; Cum- berland and Lancashire, Els 3d; Scotland, 31, using clay ironstone, and from 5s to os, using black bandlironstone— the average being 4s 10d. On iron ship plates 5s 91 wia re- present a cemmon charge for royalty ; and 35 8d to 7s 31 on steel rails, according to the ore from which they are made. . .

In Gerraany: 6d on pig iron ; Is on iron ship plates 81-cl on steel rails. The differences here given must convey at once to our minds the idea that England is not yet played out, and that we only need to set about the work at once to bring about a different state of things. Workieg-men should see that the so-called interests of the landlord and Tory classes are not British interests, nor likely at any time to farther the properity of British workmen.
