DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—The following persons were each tined for drunkenness;—William Broughton, Henry Campbell, Jokn Kennedy, Patrick Charles O'Connor, John Riley, Bridget McDonnell, Elizabeth Ellen Heath, James I Campbell, and James Highfield. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Fer committing a breach of the peace in Caroline-street on the 29th May, John Quincey was bound over to be of good behaviour.—Ellen Roach was similarly dealt with for creating a disturbance in Noah- street on the 29th May.—Catherine Simpson was ordered to find sureties to keep the peace for throwing stones, and making a disturbance in Wellington-street—For creating a breach of the peace in Paul-street on the 30th May, Mary Tame,' was ;bound over to be of good behaviour—Mary Burgess, far a like offence committed in Warrington-read on the 31st May, was bound over to keep the peace. PITCH AND Toss —Peter Pearcell, a youth, pleaded guilty Ito having. on Sunday, the 29th May, played pitch and toss in Back Midwood-streer, and he was liberated on premising not to offend again.—Thomas Hughes. who did not appear, was charged with a similar offence in Lugsdale-road on the 29.13 May, and he as fined 286 d. .

HIGHWAY OFFENCRS.—Robert Baker was mulcted in the SUM Of ss, and costs 73 6d, for being drunk and asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart in Victoria-road, Wid- nes.—lsaac Wright, a young man, was summoned for being such a distance from his horse and cart as not to have con- trol of them, at Ditton, on the 31st ult.—The defendant, who said the horse started away whilst he was loading the cart with straw, was fined 21 6d, and costs 41 6d. ASSAULT ON AN INFANT —Catherine Holland, a married woman was charged with assaulting the infant child of John woman, a labourer. Mrs. Carney and the defendant were having a quarrel, when the defendant threw a stone, which stluck the child as it reposed on its mother's arm.— The defendant, who admitted throwing the stone, but denied that the mile struck the child, was tined 10a and costs.

ASSAULT ON A BRoTHER-IN-LAW.— Rosanna Finn, a young woman, was charged with assaulting Patrick Ward. Ward, who is a labourer at the works of Messrs. Rail Bros. and Shaw, said on the 29ch May he was turning the corner of the Theatre Royal, when the defendant threw a stone at him and cruck him on the head.---The mother of the defen- dant said hr daughter had an impediment in her speech, and her right arm was paralysed. The complainant, who was her brother-in-law, was continually annoying her, and on the present occasion he aggravated her to that extent that she threw the stone.—A witness was called, who said the complainant gave Ro provocation, and the defendant was fined 5i and casts.

NEIGHBOURS AT WAR —James Simpson, a labourer, was summoned for having, on the 28th May, assaulted Thomas McGreedy. a cooper. Simpson was also charged with break- ing a pane of glass in the window of McGreedy's house. The parties live in Wellington-street, and during a quarrel it was alleged the defendant struck the complainant on the head with a stone, causing a serious wound. The defend- ant then smashed a pane of glass with his fist.—A fine of 25 6d and costs was imposed for the assault, and Is and costs for the wilful damage. DEFAMATION OF CusaacTErt.—Rosanna Fißn, the elder, was charged with using defamatory language towards Mary Ann Gill, on the 29th May, and also refusing to quit Mrs. Gill's public-house in Wellington-street. —The defendant pleaded guilty, and Mr. Knowles having stated the facts for the prosecution. the Bench imposed a fine of 105 and costs for refusing to quit, and she was ordered to find sureties to keep the peace for six months.

div.head: SAD DEATH OF MR. GEORGE CROSFIELD.
div.p: SAD DEATH OF MR. GEORGE CROSFIELD.

The death of Mr. George Crosfield, had it occurred under ordinary circumstances, and in the course of nature, would have been heard of in his native town of Warrington, which has benefitted so largely from his munificence, with the deep- est concern, but the sad event, happening as it did in the most unexpected and tragic manner, has excited feelings of the most pain- ful regret in every section of the inhabitants. From his earliest days till within a few years ago, Mr. George Crosfield lived in, or in the neighbour- hood of Warrington, but recently he has mainly re- sided in London, and it was there that his death occurred. Mr. Crosfield had been under medical treatment for many months past, his medical at- tendants being Drs. Russell. Reynolds, and Rans- ford. On Monday evening he retired to rest about nine o'clock, at his house, 109, Lancaster Gate, Bayswater. which overlooks Ilyde Park. Mrs Crosfield retired soon after, but about eleven o'clock she was aroused by a light in the room, and found that the bed furnishing on Mr. Crosfield's side of the bed were in flames. She at once aroused Mr. Crosfield and called for assistance. In answer to her cries Mr. Crosfield's servant, who slept in an ad- joining room, was quickly on the spot to render assistance, and Mr. Crosfield was placed in safety and uninjured in his dressing room. The servant then sought further assistance, and it appears that while he was doing this Mr.Crosfield returned to the bedroom, apparently to make an attempt to ex- tinguish the flames, or to seek some article from the room. At all events, on the return of the servant. accompanied by Mr. John Crosfield, junr., it was seen that the deceased gentleman had left the dres- sieg-room, and on making their way through the smoke in the bedroom they found him lying across the bed, his night dress having been entirely burnt off with the exception of the collar band. lie was at once carried down- stairs to the broad landing, wrapped in blankets, and the family physician, Dr. Ransford, sent for. Dr. Ransford was soon in attendance, and little or no hope of recovery was entertained from the first, as the patient had been completely prostrated by the nervous shock, and the burns about the body were very serious. He sank rapidly, though ap- parently suffering little pain, and died at half-past two on Tuesday morning. The news of the sad occurrence was received in Warrington early on Tuesday morning, and rapidly spread throughout the town, causing feelings of the keenest regret on every hand. Mr. Crosfield was born in Warrington, in the house in Liverpool-road now occupied by Mr. 11. B. White, in the year 1820, and about a month ago he completed his sixty- seventh year. As he grew up he received part of his education at the Friends School at Penketh, and subsequently married a daughter of Mr. Henry Ashworth, of Bolton, a gentleman who, like Mr. Crosfield himself, was in his tire a leading mem- ber of the Anti-Corn Law Association. Mr. Joseph, Crosfield, the father of deceased, was the owner of, the now well-known soap manufactory at Bank Quay, and on his father's death Mr. George Crosfield I was left while still young to take chief control of 'the concern. Mr. Crosfield was, however, endowed with rare talents for business, and under his hands the manufactory grew and prospered. Notwith- standing this his energies were by no means entirely devoted to the promotion of his private affairs, for from early life till the very close of his career he has sought to promote the public good. Along with Mr. McMinnies and the late Mr. Peter Rylands, he was one of the moat active promoters of the incor- poration of the borough, and he was chosen as a councillor. He subsequently retired from the Town Council, after having served upon it for a few years. .His services to the town, however, were by no means exhausted by his labours as a member of the municipal council, for few, if any, of the wealthier inhabitants of the town have done so much for it by generous benefactions as Mr. George Crosfield. His most notable gift was one of nearly £lO,OOO, by which the town was enabled to secure its present Town Hall and the beautiful park and recreation grounds surrounding it. With reference to the origin of the park scheme it may be of interest to state that in the first instance the Corporation had under consideration a proposal from Lord Winmar- leigh to present 'under certain conditions a meadow at Arpley for the use of the people of Warrington, This offer, however, came to nothing, the conditions not being wholly acceptable to the Corporation. Mr. George Crosfield feeling strongly that it was very desirable that the people of the town should have a park or recreation ground, had himself con- sidered as to whether Walton Lea could be converted into a park, but dismissed the idea on account of its being too far away from the town. When the Arpley proposal fell through he remarked to Mi. F.

div.p: The vote of condolence was then passed unanimously, and it was also decided to send a deputation to Mr. Cros- field's ,f uneral to represent the Liberal Association. Volun- teers for this purpose having been invited, Alderman Burges Councillor F. A. Roberts, and Councillor W. Pierpoint were ultimately deputed to represent the association. It was also understood that other members of the Liberal party would be present at the funeral. The meeting then terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman,

CHESHIRE LINES V. ORFORD.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, and resuhed in a victory for the home team. Score :—Orford, 60; Cheshire Lines, 22. WARRINGTON PRIMITIVES V. SIMMS CROSS.—Played OR the ground of the former and resulted in a win for War- rington by 19 runs. Score—Warrington, 49 ; Sirnms Cross, 30.

On Saturday, the match between Middlesex and Gloms - tersbiro was drawn in favour of the latter county, and the contest between Warwickshire and Surrey, at Biriningba.na on the same day, ended in a draw in favour of Surrey, int: home team being 57 runs behind, with only three evicke to fall. Yorkshire narrowly escaped defeat at Cambridge, as, when the stumps were pulled up and the game drawn, the University had eight wickets to fall and only 21u to get to win. It should be remembered, however, that the. county was seriously handicapped by bad weather and he_ell no possibility of winning after the first day. MR. BRIGHT AND HOME RULE. N.3lr,—ln reading your excellent article on the recant political utterances of Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain, I thought that an effective question might and ought to be put to both these gentlemen; and that is, " Did you net for years do your utmost to convert Mr. Gladstone to Home Rule ?" Of course they did. Then what painful in- consistency it is on the part of Mr. Bright to charge his convert with having suddenly turned his coat! Mr. Bright resorted to no such paltry charge against Sir Robert Peel when he turned his coat with such remarkable suddenness on the question of the Corn Laws. It is not on record that Mr. Bright saw any dagitiourtraess in the then Prime Minister's conversion, nor that it outraged his moral sensitiveness; and why? oh, why? L.

JUBILEE WEEK IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—l see you publish, in your last irsue, a letter from a Working-man" under the above heading. When I read It I was a little bit puzzled what to make of it. Just fancy a common " hand " presuming to snegest " that all em- ployers of labour in this town pay their employees the full week's wages whether closed a part or the whole of that week." Whatever can the man be thinking about ? Has he ever asked himself where the money is all to come from, when we know, because we have been told it times of times, that employers, for at least a dozen years, have been en- gaged in a losing game ? Why it is simply preposterous. Now, I put it to "A Working-man" as square as possible —noncom employers give their money away in this style, bow in the world will they manage to get all the hare neces- saries of life, such as six month's at the sea side for their families, sixpenny cigars for themselves. and champagne ad liktunt ? I say nothing of a coach and pair and a dozen flenkdis, as we all know no well-appointed household can possibly go short of these. Sir, the thing is impossible ; for further proof I ask your correspondent to look over the subscription list raised to defray the Jubilee expenses. Does he for a moment doubt that the local nobility, gents's, manufacturers, and every other grade, barring the rich and afilaent working-men would have been content to see it re- main at such a paltry figure if they had not felt poverty's cold and pinching finger? May I let a bit of a secret out, Mr. Editor? I have been engaged for some months now, along with several more chaps, trying to launch a much needed, and much-desired educational scheme. This has of course brought us in con- tact with most of our local men of light and leading, and in almost every instances we have been told that "you work- ingmen have been, during the last ten years, a deal better off than your employers." There is scarcely one of us now but what is prepared to stand an examination in etatiatice. Leone Levi, and Mr. Gillen, two experts in making twice two into nine, have been so often hurled at our heads, that we are prepared to suggest a public subscription on behalf of the local geetry ; and mannfacturers.because on no ac- count should their wills tot up to less than £89,000. lam afraid the disciples of Herbert Spencer are on the in- crease, especially amongst the Loyal and Patriotic. No end of shouting and Primrose meetings. Those who get these meetings up get their money's worth in return, by leading workingmen by the nose; but ask them to subscribe to some thing of permanent value, and they are shocked, and in Spence:lan terms refuse to " pauper'we the people." - COLIN CLOUT.

GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board' was bald at the Schools, Great Sankey, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs Turner (chairman), W B Kerfoot, J C Ridg• way, J Cook, W P Boughton, and S Sutton, (clerk.) ALTERATIONS.—The Clerk read the following minutes:— At an adjourned meeting of the Board bald on the 14th May a letter addressed to the Clerk by Mr. Ridgway, was read in which be stated that he had seen Mr. Jeans upon the subject of the removal of t :le wall at the schools. In the course of conversation Mr. Jeans stated that for the present he would be satisfied '•,e Board would take down the boundary wall as far as the inner gateway, put it back the requisite distance and cinder half the proposed street so far as it was co-extensive with this portion. He also wished the Board if they would do so to replace the present high -wall by a low wall with coping and railing similar to that upon the north front. After discussion the Board agreed to accept the above proposal and also to make the change in the formation of the wall as requested. Upon the proposi- tion of Mr. Ridgway, seconded by Mr. Houghton, it was re- solved that Mr. W Owen. architect, be instructed to prepare a plan of the proposed alterations and obtain a tender for the work for Mr. Collin, builder. Mr. Kerfoot was empow- ered to employ labour to remove the shrubs adjoining the Portion of the wall tabs set back to another part of the ' land.—At another adjourned meeting of the Board held on the 19th May, Mr. Owen, architect, attended with plan of the proposed alterations and estimates for the work sent in by Mr. Collin. After consideration of the same it was re- solved to accept tenders as under : 1, removal of wall, £2l 108; 2, removal of gateway, £1 15s Pd; 3, cindering half street. £2; total, £25. Mr. Owen was instrocted to inform Mr. Collin of the foregoing and to prepare the necessary specifications, dm. It was reselved that the cost of the al- teration be defrayed cat of the building loan so far as it would meet the case and that the balance be charged to re- pairs.—These minutes were confirmed. FINANCE, &c.—The CLERK reported that the balanOe in the treasurer's hand in favour of the Board was £164 13s Bd. £l2O had been paid to the credit of the Board by the over- seers and £l3 13s by the bead-master as school fees.—The CHAIRMAN I expect we shall have plenty of money to carry us through.—The CLERK said they should have suffi- cient to take'them'to the end of the year comfortably,ancttbe next call would be very light unless something unexpected turned up.—The CLERK also reported that the number of scholars on the books on the 14th June was 262. Thirty- one girls had joined since the beginning of the year in addi- tion to those they had previously.—The CHAIRMAN re- marked that the number of scholars had increased in a very satisfactory manner. THE LATE BAZAAR,-A letter to the chairman signed A M Bidaway. was read. It asked the chairman to convey to the Board the thanks of herself and those who bad assisted her in the bazaar, held in the Board School which had con- , tributed so much to the bazaar's success.—The CHAIRMAN said he was glad that the bazaar was a success, and he hoped that the new schools would be a success. He was pleased that they had decided to have schools of their own rather than go into the Board Schools; he thought it would be more satisfactory. TEE ATTENDANCE OFFICER.—Mr.KERFOOT said that he 'would bring the matter of the remuniation of the attendance ,nlßeer forward at the next meeting. TEE SEWING MISTRESS.—For the post of sewing mistress which had been advertised there were five applicants, and it was decided that three of them should be asked to wait upon the Board at its next meeting. This was all the business of public interest.

Snocrana TRIPLE MIIIIDEII AT Cotwv..—On Saturday I night Colne, near Burnley, was the scene of a terrible triple murder. In the afternoon a weaver named Rushton, living I at Waterside, Colne went with his wife Harriet and his I three children, aged seven, five and two and a half, for a walk. He left them shortly before four o'clock to go to his club, the wife returning home. At six o'clock the wife went to a sitter living in Skipton-road, and told her she bad sent all her children to heaven. The two sisters went back to -the house, and on a bed lay the three children dead and laid oat. A. small rope, part of a clothes line, was found near, with which the mother had strangled them. Mrs Rushton is about 35 Sir f age. It is said that two near relatives of the woman committed suicide.—On Monday, Harriet Rushton, aged 87, of Lenches„ was brought op at the Colne Police Court, charged with the murder of her three chil- dren, aged five years, three years, and two years respectively. Alfred Stoddard. brother Li-law, said the prisoner came to his house on Saturday night, and, placing a key on the dresser, said, "Give that to Jack," meaning her husband. She then turned to go away, but his wife called her back. Prisoner replied, "No," and walked away. They both fol- lowed her, and Mrs. Stoddard asked where the children were, to which the accused replied, "They are in Heaven. I knew your child was in Neaven, and I wanted mine to go there, too." Further evidence having been given as to the finding of the bodies, prisoner was remanded until Wednes- UT, pending the inquest.—Further investigations tend to I show that the prisoner's mind, was unhinged when she com- mitted the terrible deed. Her mother committed suicide two years ago by hanging herself, and a year before that a brother drowned himself in the Faubridge reservoir. The woman herself has been unwell for several weeks, the com- plaint being chiktly with respect to her head, and she lived with tier sister up to a few days ago, being attended by a doctor. The general impression is that she had taken the children upstairs singly, and strangled them with part of a clo';_ies line which was found in the room.—On Tuesday, in rho noine Police Court, an inquest was held on the bodies ~j 'h, three children. The jury returned a verdict of wilful rnutrer, but expressed the unanimons opinion that the woman was of unsound mind at the tires. The Coroner said that W4ll a matter for another court to inquire into. The jary also exoressed their sincere sympathy with the family aud relatives.

div.head: SHIP CANAL SCHEME -ISSUE
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME -ISSUE
OF PREFERENCE SII ARES.

In a circular which is being issued by the Direc- tors to applicants for shares in the Manchestrr Ship Canal Company important statements are made with regard to the position of the undertaking. and certain financial arrangements which have been provisionally made are unanimously recommended for approval. The total amount of ordinary shares allotted and applied for up to the present date is upwards of £3,000,000. Applications are still coming in, and the Directors say they have little doubt that the total subscriptions in Lancashire and the neighbouring counties will not fall far short, of £4,000,000. As the Company is required by section 38 of its Act of 1885 to raise before the 6th of August next £5,000,000 of share capital in addition to the moneys required for the purchase of the Bridgewater undertaking, the Directors, acting upon the advice of experienced authorities, and folio Ning the plan adopted with great pecuniary advantage by many large and prosperous companies, have de- cided to advise the issue of the other half of the company's capital, viz., £4,000,000, as preference shares bearing 4 per cent. interest during the con- struction of the works, and afterwards 5 per cent. per annum in 'perpetuity. The Directors have had an offer from responsible capitalists to take the whole of the proposed issue of 1,4,000,000 preference shares. This offer they have accepted, stipulating that when the preference shares are offered pub- licly, special consideration shall be given to appli- cations from the holders et, ordinary shares. The Directors have decided to seek Parliamentary powers to enable the Company to divide its share capital into one-half ordinary and one-half 1 preference. On Wednesday, in the House of Commons, Mr. W. H. Houldsworth moved that the StandinA Orders be suspended, and that leave be given taking in a Jill to enable the Manchester Shrip Canal Company to raise a portion of their caJital by means of pre- ference shares. The hon. member stated that the efforts made to raise the necessary capital' had re- sulted in very nearly £4,000,000 being subscribed to- wards the £8,000,000 of share capital that is required for the undertaking in Lancashire alone. Upon some members raising objections, Mr. Jacob Bright remarked that the only motive for pressing,the matter forward so rapidly was that they must raise the capital before the Gth of August, or the. whole scheme would collapse. Baron H. de Worms suggested that the measure should be postponed for a week, as no notice had been given of it. hlr. Whitley thought serious consideration was required before the House departed from the principles followed in these cases, The, promoters of the measure were, he said, seeking to introduce an entirely new- principle. The Standing Order was then suspended, and the bill was read a first time. Mr. 116uldsworth said he had intended to move the second reading on the following day (Thursday);. but as the Government wished for further delay h was willing to postpone the discussion until Mon day. They were in a position to, raise the whole capital for this great undertaking if the bill was ' passed within the next two or three weeks; but if lit was postponed beyond that time and their powers lapsed; the whole of the enormous expenditure con- nected with the Act would be entirely lost. He should be glad if the House would rake the second reading on Monclay.—Mr. John Morl*y thought the compromise proposed a reasonable, one, and he hoped it would be accepted. Baron de Worms again complained that his -department had not been consulted, and he thought it, not unreasonable that there should be a week's delay. He would consent to the proposal on the understanding that the ~ discussion'would not take any great length of time. The second reeding was thempostponed till Monday. _ ___

MEETING AT WARRINGMN. On Thursday afternoon, a meeting of the local Executive Committeewas held in the Council Cham- ber at the Town Hall, Warrington, for the purpose. of receiving an important comixiunication from the. Ship Canal directors, air. R. A. Naylor presided, and there were also present Messra. F. Monks, J.. 1 Pierpoint„ C. J. Morris, J. Fairclough, J. Hutchings, J. Geddes,. G. Hatch:. and J. L. Tumtall (sec.)—A letter was ;read from Alderman Burgess stating that he would, be unable to be present owing to being compelled to go out of the town.—The communica.- don from the Ship Canal directors read as follows.: —"lt is most important that we should obtain the support of as many members of Parliament as possible for the second reading of our bill next Mon- day. If you have not a meeting of' your Committee to-marrow or on:Friday, kindly see individual mem- bers who have influence with members of Parlia- ment, and get them to communicate with those gentlemen. Ptease ask your committee not to relax their efforts to obtain further applications for shares; and also note that it is absolutely necessary for us to get the new conditions confirmed promptly by each applicant upon the form that will be sent to him.—Yours truly, MEIIiSHALL STEVENS.— A circular from the Board of Directors was also read. It stated that the total amount of ordinary shares allotted and applied' for up to the.present date is upwards of £3,000,000. Applications are still coming in, and the directors have little doubt that the total subscriptions in Lancashire and the neighbouring counties will not fall far short of £4,000,000. The directors, as well as the Consulta- tive Committee, have every reason to believe that the canal will at an early date pay more than five per cent-, and it is therefore manifest that by issu- ing one-half the capital at a fixed rate of five per cent. the dividend upon the remaining half will be materially increased. JOOEPH SM:TEI.—On Monday evening a special meeting of the Lymm Tontine Seciery was held at the Coffee Tavern, the object being to elect a treasurer in place of the late Mr. Aseph Smith, who occupied that posi- ' tine up to the time of his death. Mr. J. Miss Annie Readett, Miss Mary Gilberts, and Master Walter Moston also sang in a piece for the school, and the choir and school filled up the choruses. Mr. G. Brereton gave very effectively the recitation "By Alarm River." The collections for the day amounted to £l9 Ts 2d.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. Their Lordships met at 4-0. EnvPr.—The Marquis of SALISBURY, replying to Lord' Carnarvon, said the Convention with regard to the oocupa• tion of Egypt had been signed between England and the Porte, but required ratification by the other Powers. The British troops were to be withdrawn within three years- of ratification, but the country might be re-occupied in certain contingencies. The consent of the Porte was not necessary before England re-occupied Egypt, and England would have to be sole judge of the necessity for such occupation. The Suez Canal was to remain open to all persons, and at all. times. The Report of the Tithe Rest Charge Bill was received and agreed to, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. FREE TRADE.—Mr. BROOKFIELD gave notice that, on an early day, while approving of the system of Free Trade, he should move that the time had come when the House should consider whether important reforms should not be made in the fiscal policy to which this country adhered. COERCING THE COMMONS. Mr. W. H. fenturn moved that at 10 p.m on Friday, the 17th June, if the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill be not previoes'y reported to the House, the chairman should forthwith put the question to enable that being done. He made the motion solely for public and wit party welfare. Four months of the session had been consumed, and practically nothing had been done It was the duty of the Government to see that peblic busi- ness was not paralysed, while the Government had the sanction of the majority of that House and of public , opinion.—Mr. GLADSTONE took exception to some of Mr. I Smith's remarks, and expressed that making a charge of oberruction against a minority was not the best way of facilitating business. He thought the hest way to expedite I business was to make the bill temporary instead of per- manent, to strike out of it all that affected combination apart from crime, and to give the Irish tenant the same freedom as was enjoyed by the English artiean.—Mr. FAR. NELL denied that the present was a proper time for making such proposal. If it was agreed to, Parliamentary discussion would become a mockery. He concluded by moving an amendment to leave out all the words after the word ' " that " in order to insert the following :—" Inasmuch as the Criminal La* Amendment (Ireland) Bill was designed to deprive the Irish people permanently of their constitu- tional rights, this House declines to sanction the propold- sloe of her Majesty's Government to deprive the Chair- • man, duriag the discussion in committee on the bill, of the power which, since the commencement of this diectission, the Chairman has felt called upon repeatedly to exercise in opposition to her Majesty's Government for the protection of freedom of debate in that House and the maintanecce of the rights of mieerities."—After a short discussion as to the manner in which the amsndment should be put, Mr. Swan justiti.d the proposal he had mad, and repudiated charges Mr. Parnell had made against the Government.— Sir W. LAWSON supported the amendment, because he looked upon it as a vote of confidence in the chair.—The amendment was also supported by Mr. Bradlangh, Mr. T. Healy, Sir W. Harcourt. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, H. Cesham, while Mr. Goschen spoke in favour of the motion of the Government.
THE JUBILEE CELEBR&TION.

A meeting of the Lvmm General Jubilee Committee was held in the Parochial School, on Thursday evening, the Rev. G W. Guest occupying the chair. There was a good attendauce.—The Chairman read a letter that he bed re- ceived from the tradesmen of Lynam, stating that they had formed themselves into a committee for the purpose of de- corating the village on the day of the Jubilee, and asking for a donation towards the expense that would he incurred. The matter was deferred until it should be ascertained what will be the cost of the medals and the school treats.—lt was reported that the procession committee had decided upon the following route : rho Church of England and Wes- leyan Schools to start at the Cross, proceed up Eagle Brow, where thy will be joined hy the Congregational School, and then walk to Statham-lane, returning along Booth's- lane,Top-lane. past the church,through Oughtrington,Sandy• lane, and Rush Green, and back over Lymm Bridge to the Cross. The Old Hundred and a version of the National Anthem will be suog at the Cross, The Baptists do not intend to take any part in the procession, giving it AS their reason that they have no one to look after the children.— Mr. Cameron stated that nine gentlemen had promised to lend lurries.—Mr. Ridgway, the treasurer, reported that the total amount subscribed was £lO6, but other subscriptions were promised.—lt was stated that there would be L 335 children and teachers who would take part in the proces- sion, and as this number WAS greater than was anticipated, it was decided to order 2,000 medals, instead of 1,440, as previously determined upon.—The Surveying Committee reported that the, were unable to arrange for the provision of a tea in the field, and they, therefore, recommended that scholars should have tea at their respective schools, and that 9d per bead be allowed towards the expenses.—After some discussion the recommendation of the committee was adopted, with the exception that 10d, instead of 91, be be allowed for each scholar.—This was the principal busi- ness.
SHIP CANAL MEETING

On Wednesday evening a meeting, called by requisition, was held in the Plough Hotel, Lymm, with the object of furtheking the interests of the Manch,ster Ship Canal scheme. The chair was occupied by Mr. H. Cameron, chairman of the Local Board, and there was a good attend- ance. Mr. Crossley, one of the directors of the Ship Canal Company. aaended to explain the objects and prospects of the company. The Chairman explained that the meeting had been called in resoonse to a requisition presented to him, very largely signed by the residents of Lyrnm, the object being to do what they could to further the objects of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme, and to do what Lymm could in the way of raising additional capital. A very large amount had been already subscribed, but a large amount was still requited, and now seemed to be the time to bring the mat- ter prominently before the people of Lymm. He hoped the result of their deliberations would be to add very largely to the number of subscribers. and very materially to increase the amount of stock. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt at all that when once the canal was made great benefit would arise to the people of the districts affected, and Lymm would benefit proportionately with the rest. They in Lymtn were hoping that when the canal was maCe they would be relieved somewhat of their heavy rates, and he fancied that the construction of the canal would relieve the labour market in that district, where they bad a large population nearly driven from their employment. (Applause.) Mr. Rogers then proposed " That this meeting learns with satisfaction that applications nave been obtained for more than £3,000.000 sterling for the construction of the Ship Canal and pledges itself to a determined effoet to aesist the directors to obtain at least £4,000.000 in the- district." He said many owners of railway stock did not apply for shares in tbiescheme because they thought that when the canal was completed and at work, it would reduce the per- centage of their dividends by taking away traffic from the railway. No dbubt there were grounds for that suspicion on the;r part, and it was ninny clear that some traffic- would be diverted from the railways in some districts, notably between Manchester and Liverpool, but it WAS also equally clear that the increase of traffic on other portions ef the raliwlty eystem would eventually more than compensate for any reduction in the trail% ef this short section that would be affected by the canal. (Hear, hear.) Yncleed, the bsst thing that these nee:holders could do Vas to invest largely in the canal for the purpose of insuring themselves from any loss or-income through the loss of traffic they feared on the railway ; this scheme mast necessarily ply a much larger dividend than any railway investment possibly could. (Hear. Hear.) lie pointed out that there would be a resit decrease in the rates of transit as compared with thane now charged by railway companies. Me thought that In, ten years after the opening of the canal, ftershares would be worth, £5O: ( APPNnse ) Mr. E. Brown seconded the resolution, saying that be had fall confidence in the Ship. Canal scheme, and in its ulti- mate success.. After it had fought so many battles, and bad won so many victories, they had no fear as to its ulti- mate result. (Hear, hear.) Those who conducted their business upon fair and honest principles need not fear any- thing from theiconstructiore of this canal. Only the extor- tioner and oPpressor need fear competition. (Hear,. hear.) They believed the canal would not only be for the good of Lancashire but of Cbesbire and that Lymm wield partici- pate in the benefits. (Appianse.) Mr. W. J. Crossley, one of the directors of the Ship Canal Company, spoke at considerable length in support of the motion. Ire said the sabeme was one of the grandest brought before this country for many years. No scheme had been so thoroughly probed and "bottomed," or so thoroughly investigated, as this one had. (Hear. hear.) ' The carat would be of great benefit to this district. It would raise the value of property, and would find addi- tional employment for the inhabitants. He then quoted figures showing the immense traffic there would be on the canal if constructed`, and contended that the canal was hound to pay a good dividend. In answer to a question, Mr. Croueley said that they had not yet had any transfers of shares, but it was tiought that that would prove a very small matter, about which there would be no difficulty. (Hear, hear.) Mr. 'X% J. Ridgway proposed that a number of gentlemen be appointed a committee, with power to add to their num- ber, to take such action as they might consider expedient to assist the directorsof 'the Ship Canal in raising the capital recinited, and to use their best endeavours to carry out the terms of the tirat resolution. This resolution was seconded by Mr. T. Ardern, rod car- ried with applause, after which the meeting terminated with a note of thanks to the chairman.

At Whitehaven, on Thursday, John Connolly, who was charged with baying caused the death of his wife by burn- my ber in a cru,l manner, was again before the magistrates. The evidence was insufficient to warrant farther proceed- ings, and Canoe/1y was liberated. On Wednesday, a letter was received in Belfast from Mr. Bright, who, after criticising Mr. Gladstone's recent refer- ences to. the nationality of Wale, and his omission to men- tion the loyalists of Ireland, said it was sad that an ex- Minister should descend to artifices so transparent." A THIEVING POLICEMAN.—At Bolton, on Thursday, a borough constable, named Haycock, was committed for trial on a charge of being concerned in a number of burglaries in the Peen and district. It was stated in court that a large quantity cf stolen goods had been found in the prisoner's honsa. The Cabinet had a meeting on Thursday. Lord Harting- ton and Mr. Chamberlain bad on the previous day informed certain members of the Government of the strong antipathy of some of their sspporters to the venue clause of the Crimes Bill, and it is understood that the Cabinet have now decided to abandon the clause.
FRODSHAM.

- - Sr. JOHN THE EVANGELIST CHURCH, EINGSLEY.—H is intended to hold a grand bazaar in aid of the endowment of this church at Belle Mante.Ovetton Hills, on the 14th, 15th, and 16th July. ANNIVERSARY SERMONS, HELSBY.—Two sermons were preached on bunday in the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, fielaby, by Mr. R. Kniveton, of Euncorn, when appropriate hymns were song by the choir. The collections, which amounted to MI, were in aid of the funds of the Sunday school. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES —At a meeting of the Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship Parochial Committees, held in the Town Hall, Frodsham„ on Friday evening, Mr. A. Thomas (chairman); the Clerk read a letter from Mr. 11. Bancroft informing the committee that he would prepare a report in detail to forward to the Local Board on the Frodsham water scheme for £3 3s, inclusive of all expenses. After some discussion, it was decided to defer the matter until the next meeting. The Inspector of Nuisances reported that the work of extension of sewer at Overton and cleansing of sewage tank would be commenced at the beginning of the coming week.

RUNCORN AND TEIE QUEEN'S JUBILEE. The arrangements for the celebration in Runcorn of the jubilee of her Majesty's reign are nearly completed. A fortnight ago there was published in this journal the vari- ous particulars as to the processions of the friendly socie- ties in the morning, and the Sunday scholars in the after- noon. It is estimated that in the latter there will be 5500 persons of all ages, and the committee have decided to allow to each school sd, per bead Vs defray the cost of the treat. This will absorb £ll5 of the £l6O collected. A further sum of £35 is set aside for the treat to the aged poor, of whom there are.expectNl to be 500. This, one of the most interesting features of the demonstration' will take place on Wednesday, the 22nd, in the Public Hall. A surplus of LW-will dins be available for other purposes, and. the Ceremonies Committee have recommended that the eyes of the children shall be feasted with a grand display of fireworks at desk. It may he stated that the public bodies in the town will no doubt take part in the-afternoon's procession,and the Runcorn companies of the Cheshire Volunteers have been invited to do likewise. As the procession will be of great length. Superintendent Nellingworth has been asked to stop vehicu- lar traffic for the occasion, and also to keep the Market Hall and its approaches free from all obstructions, so that. the scholars can assemble there without confusion. It is at tUe spot that the "Old Hundred " and the "National Anthem" are to be sung, and the effect of so many voices singing in unison "God Save our gracious Queen" will, no doubt, be unique and impressive.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT. OF -A CASH BOX, AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT. OF -A CASH BOX, AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, Henry Brassington, junior, Lugsdale, Wid- nes, and Jonathan Hurst, shoemaker, of Macclesfield, were charged with having some time between. Saturday night, the 4th inst...and Monday morning, the 6th inst., molen a ; cash box containiag about £5 from the Boilermakers' Arms, , Lugsdale, occupied by James Penny. On the application of Inspector Maybe, Hurst was discharged, as no evidence could be offered against him. Mr. H. L. Riley defended Brassington.—The evidence showed that the cash box was placed in a drawer of the bar after clos- ing time on Saturday night, and its disappearance was not discovered until Monday morning. On Saturday night Brassington was in the house, and paid off a score of 10a which he owed for drink supplied the previous week. At a later time he returned and said he was spent up, and had several pints of beer placed to his credit. On the same day the prisoner was at the Volunteer Inn, Lugsdahr, where he was asked to pay a debt of Ts, but the prisoner replied that he bad bad a poor week, and would pay on the follow- ing Saturday. On Sunday Brassington and Hurst were again at the Boilermakers' Arms, where after having some- thing to drink, Brassington called Hurst into the yard and said, "I reckon you are hard up ?," Hurst •'Yes,' and Brassington gave him 3s. The p n went to the Volunteer Innorbere Brassington paid re,pirliethd, e off his "shot" of 7s, and purchased a pint of rum besides paying for other drinks. The prosecutor and his wife each gave Brassington a good character. There was no lock on the froat door, and any person who wished to enter had only to lift up the latch in order to fulfil his purpose.—The Bench were of opinion that although there was grave sus- picion against the prisoner, the evidence was such that no jury would convict an he would be discharged.—Mr. Riley said he was in a position to prove that the money Brassington had in his possession on Sunday he had saved up for the purpose of going to camp with the Volunteers, and be had not carried out his intention,

THE JUBILEE CELEMIATION AT WiNwrcx.—The parishioners of Winwick intend to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee on the 21st inst., in the following manner. At eleven o'clock in the morning there will be Divine service in the Parish Church, accord- ing to the form ordered by the Queen in Council. ' Prom three to eight o'clock p.m., the grounis of Winwick Hall will ,be open, and the parishioners and other members of the congregation will be wel- comed there. Tea will be provided by the members of the Sunday and ' day schools, and refreshments for other visitors. There will also be sports of vari- ous kinds, games, music, and dancing. THE MARRIAGE OF MISS REYNOLDS.. DINNER: TO, WORKMEN'. In connection with the marriage of his.daqghter,. on, 'Ai& previous Thursday, Captain Reynolds on Saturday evening entertained his workmen and the committee who put up the decorations on the oeca- siotrof the marriage to dinner in one of the rooms of the works. The decorations had been-carried out .by•a.cominittee consisting of Messrs. John Hartley' (chairman), F. J. Dell, Lownds; Wheeler, Watkinson, IHumphreys, and Banning.. The chair an Saturday evening was occupiedlby Mr: Coxon, and the vice- chair-by Mr. Hartley, andrfrom, 40 to 50 'workmen, and others were present. Mr. Thomas- Ireland, of the Cheshire Cheese, Latchford, catered for the dinner. After dinner various toasts were proposed; The Chairman gave the health of the bride and bride- groom and observed that they all felt a- certaiu. amount of regret when they remembered that they would now so seldom see, Mrs. Snowden-in Latch-- ford. Most present had received somekindness-at her hands at one time or other, and though:they would 'seldom see her amongst them they wished her • every possible happiness during her married life. (Applause.)—Three cheers having beengiven for Mr...and Mrs. Snowd'eni.Mr: Hartley said he had- received a letter from the bride,, and upon the en- velope were the words, "TO Mr... John Hartley. To be read on Saturday to my friends."' The letter read as.follows-:--•' Ist June, 18877. My dear friends,—l. wished-very miich to have- thanked, yow personally ' for the-handsome and useful case, you have given me aswwedding present, but as I have much to-do- to-dav, and' to-morrow is my-wedding' day, .I Write this letter, which I request Mr. Hartley to read to you at' the dinner my father is giving-yowen Satur- day. Yourpresent shall alWays-treasure as a gift from:those amongst whom I have lived, and from whom-I: have always received :kindness and respect; • and it will remind me of yOu:and.yours. I.hope to' ' see • you all again when I re-visit the happy home I; -am leaving.to-morrow. With every wish- for your happiness, Lam ray dear friends, yours sincerely, BRATETCE RUYNOLDS" (AppktiSe.) He '(Mr. Hartley) knew that what they. mild- do would not be of great intrinsic value,, but their present was given sincerely- and spontaneously, and from the heart, and'therefore it was a genuine gift. • Whtin the matter was mooted the-response was unanimous, and'every matestrove to show-in the best manner he could his-recognition of a young lady who was held.; in such, high.reiard. (Hear; hear.), He-had been in the township. 2'2 years, and he had known Captain and Miss Reyqolds nearly-the whole of • the time,, both of whom.were highly respected for their kind and: benevolent acts. (Applause.)—Captain Rey- nolds (who only remained in. the room-a short taime), said hewas sorry he was not quite. well enough to-1 have dinner-with them,.but he could assure them' that of allthearticles-that were given to his'daugh- ter—and-there- were many—none-were so much ap- preciated as those forwarded by-the people in the house and the neighbours- and Ivorkpeople. (Ap- plause.)- To her they-were. of much greater value- than the more costly presents, because they would remind her or the people she daily saw, and' whom she loved'from the bottom, of 'her heart.. While at home the greatest wish of her lift had been to help those amongst whom she lived; and' he was sure they wonld all pin with him,in- wishing hey much happiness, (Applause.) She had desired him- to thank them, for the-demonstration made in her favour on Thursday.—Three cheers were thewgiven for Captain. Reynolds, and "one for Mrs. Reynolds." Other toasts were given airing the evening,, as well as several' songs by Mr. Bark, M'. Banning. Mr. Dell, the vice-elkeirmani. GroundS, and' Mr., B. Rey- noldkihn,
